A small party of theirs made out into this now unknown land with their strange dwellings. Through the treeless forest they went and spoke to the local forestry commissioner. In a room filled with strange smoke from a cigarette they pleaded their case, and then they were forced to wait.

In the meantime the ranchers decided to halt their advances. The scouting parties ceased for now as the situation hung in the balance. In the end the forestry minister reached a split decision. He rejected the appeal from the tribe but even in that smokey room he could not live with ruining the lives of the tribe who came to him directly. If the ranchers continued then there would be so many other issues to deal with. On his desk was a memorandum he had written to the Serviço de Proteção ao Índio, the SPI. It called for a cessation of deforestation around their villages noting the substantial depletion of the rainforest in that area. He took another drag of his cigarette and got back to reviewing other forestry permits. After all, even if forestry could not continue here there were always other places to log.
strings.BRA_deforestation.2.a: They will not cross it. For now at least.
strings.BRA_deforestation.3.desc:
His body was carried back to camp by his tribe to a temporary home — a permanent grave. Spear wound, a rarity that would become increasingly common in the coming days. All the other dead men and women buried deep found their end with bodies occupied by foreign lead, the unsaid warning for the approaching invasion of their land.

It first was a trickle, then came the flood. Logging operations tore down their homes as the families who came out were met with the might of the Mauser — the only clarion call to vacate. Spears and arrows provided their response — some felt like they killed one or two of the rancher's thugs — but any victory on their behalf was wholly pyrrhic.

Their warriors were slaughtered in the first battle of the war, taken by surprise as the self-proclaimed forces of civilization took their homes. After that first glorious salvo, they were on the run. The only advantage they had left was their knowledge of the beautiful land that was rapidly losing the meaning of home. Still, it was only a temporary advantage — and one that other enemies shared.

These days, they were not fighting the murderous government-sponsoredproxies of the ranchers but their fellow tribes. Their long march led to skirmishes with others — a spearhead lodged in someone's throat — the bloody gurgles of the almost-dead — a mother crying for her lost son. They would return for revenge, but what could they do but press forward?

Now they stood. The wounded who had expired upon or after revival found themselves buried. Memorials were placed for those whose corpses would be bulldozed into the Earth, now only nourishment for the soil. All that could be done is to wait by the river — waiting for a fresh new hell to confront them...
strings.BRA_deforestation.3.a: ...knowing there would never be enough land to sate their greed.
strings.BRA_deforestation.4.desc:
It was inevitable. Their latest plot of land, formerly known as home, had been seized by men who waved their papers and guns in their faces. Faces pointed deep into the Amazon, they marched until their feet were bloody. Other tribes watched on unsympathetically, all with one thought circulating their minds: “Better them than us,” knowing the same fate would eventually come for them.

Disease stalked them along the way to their new home, in truth, only a place to lay their heads. This time, they weren't met with hostiles but those who took pity upon them. Riddled with illness, the tribe could not refuse the condescension of the Church, treating their members with what little they had. Any pride left had evaporated. This was their subsistence — charity — their life support.

The Church was content to whisper sweet little proselytizations into their ears as they tended to their wounds, gathering a few more believers for the flock. The preachers left, their calling card consisting of a half-dozen small black leather-bound Bibles. This would not be their only visitor.

A man from the New York Times, his ill-suited clothes covered in mud, visited them. His pen and paper jotted down their situations, their hardships, and their memories, all singing out of broken faces. They told him everything, and in return, they were given a pittance. They could not say no but remained hopeful his story would tell the world of their plight.

Exiting into self-proclaimed civilization, the journalist made his way to a fast-food outlet, a recent addition to the locale thanks to the efforts of hard-working ranchers. He walked inside and sat down, ordering off the menu one very reasonably priced hamburger. The wrapped piece of greasy meat was devoured whole by his maw before leaving. The tribe would never hear from him again.
strings.BRA_deforestation.4.a: On Page 34, a tiny column on the tribe is buried next to an advertisement for McDonald's.
strings.BRA_deforestation.5.desc:
How could a land he lived in his whole life become so alien to him? The tribal elder had known nothing else but this forest, and now it seemed he would outlive the land that gave his people their power. Scavengers and thieves extracted every ounce of pride, every inch of their soul, and the worst part was he barely knew why.

Conflict between other tribes happened, but he could at least understand why it did. They suffered the same attacks as his tribe, growing slowly more insular day by day, territorial of what beautiful land still remained theirs. How could he blame them? They saw what was happening to his tribe.

The only help left for them was from the ever-so condescending missionaries from the Church. Every member of the tribe bar him had left with their assistance. They may have protested, some may have held out for longer than others, but as another rancher took away another part of their life, another life seemed preferable.

He knew it would only be a death of another kind, a delayed passing of everything he held true to his soul.

Maybe they still had time for a new life, but not him. He would not let this world continue to rob him of everything. He would stand here as the invaders arrived and let them bear witness to the last representative of his people. Whatever happens next, the forest will consume him and his memories, and he will be remembered by it eternally, if by no one else.
strings.BRA_deforestation.5.a: Stripped of everything but his identity, a final possession delivered with him to the grave.
strings.BRA_deforestation.6.t: The Priest and the Estranged Congregation
strings.BRA_deforestation.6.desc:
The church creaked. The roof still had a couple of leaks that were being tended to but the janitorial staff were doing their very best to make the hall fitting for the press. There were rows of chairs laid out and Wilson Pinheiro and his men were laid out neatly with a row of tables in front of them. It was complete with name cards and even a banner that read “Brasiléia Rural Workers Union,” the name they had settled on. Yet most of the chairs were bare. It seemed as though a handful of local journalists reporting news in Acre were the only ones who had turned up. As minutes passed Pinheiro decided to start. There was some press here. It would not be all for nothing. He knocked the microphone in front of him. He had expected the loud noise it would make but was nonetheless taken off guard by it.

“Let's begin then. I am here before you as a humble rubber tapper. They may call me a traitor, a backwards thinking old fool who can't understand the times today. But I'm here to tell you that I just want to protect my livelihood. The ranchers as they spread out slashing and burning their way across the jungle stand as a direct threat to me, to my family, to our future. We do not intend to stand by and let them destroy our livelihood.”

“Today I am pleased to announce the formation of the Brasiléia Rural Workers Union, and we will use this new union to ensure we have a future here with our families on our land. To all of you, rubber tappers, farmers in the jungle, all of us who make our lives in this jungle you are not alone. Together we can ensure a future for all of us, if we just work together we can save our land, our homes, our future.”

He stopped. There was scattered applause from the other associates from the Union, his comrades. The priest also offered applause. Yet there was something so lonely in standing up for change in such a church with no congregation.
strings.BRA_deforestation.6.a: The embers of change are often lonely.
strings.BRA_deforestation.7.t: Lives and Livelihood on the Line
strings.BRA_deforestation.7.desc:
Never before had so many people been in this place before. The Rural Workers Union was out in force, marshaled by their leader Wilson Pinheiro. They moved as one to intercept another army. They knew this was where the loggers were going to hit next. Scouting parties had been penetrating into this part of the jungle for weeks. They had already started to destroy the forest, pushing deeper and deeper into the once untouched land. Land that was legally off limits to any further logging operations. Not that the law would stop the loggers, but perhaps the bodies of the rural workers' union would prevent the loggers from reaching their goal. That was the intent of the union, as they lined up, filling the roads preventing the passage of any vehicle. The logistic lines cut they turned to the loggers currently at work. A single brave union man even put his body before a chainsaw, his life put at risk to protect his livelihood. In the end the forest remained.

A journalist for the local A Tribuna newspaper stood and saw the protest taking place. He had heard of the establishment of the Union from a news column far down on one of his competitors. He had written them off as another fringe movement unlikely to make much real progress. They were standing against the ranchers, the loggers, all of those large industrial interest groups. Yet while their enemies were richer with more connections at the end of the day there was no substitute for raw human bodies as he thought about how to word his report on the event.

Past the forest and far out of earshot of the commotion the tribe continued to live in relative peace. Able to find nourishment in the bounty of the still untouched rainforest living as their ancestors had for generations before them.
strings.BRA_deforestation.7.a: They'll have to go through us!
strings.BRA_deforestation.8.desc:
The detective dragged on his cigarette as he began his examination. A single gunshot wound to the back of the head noted as the likely cause of death. His body was slumped down to the side, in a fetal position. This was not a murder was his first thought, it was an execution. Lying in an alleyway with the door of the rural workers' union just out of eyeshot. So it goes, hardly an uncommon story in Acre today.

Just this week there had been another case. Two members of the Brasiléia Rural Workers Union had been found dead in a ditch by the side of a dirt road. The injuries lined up perfectly. Gunshot wound to the back of the head laid in their side like this. The positions as if released from restraints betrayed the manner of the murder. The manner of the execution. The week before that too. Blood running down our streets.

The blood itself running into ditches and down alleyways. He let out a sigh as the previous cases had conditioned him to know that the investigations would be short. He could already see the Police Chief sitting in his chair, cigar in hand, commenting about how muggings always seem to end in murders these days. Maybe he'd ask me to blame rowdy teenagers that time. Maybe an escaped bull from a ranch. So he gave his report once again, and once again he was told to investigate local criminal gangs. Yet he had resigned himself to the same investigation as before. Even with the brazenness of the murder, the stature of the victim it was the same.

He thought about it, about asking the ranchers and trying to identify the bullet casing he had found. Were he to, then the next bullet casing would be laid next to his own lifeless body. He took a drag of his cigarette and got to work. The fires of another controlled burn at the edge of a rancher's field raged on. There were no protests, no men in front of chainsaws this time. If the ranchers were good at anything it was clearing anything in their way after all.
strings.BRA_deforestation.8.a: And so the smoke hangs in the air.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.1.desc:
When Jânio da Silva Quadros had last left the presidential office in the Planalto Palace, he had not truly thought upon the possibility that he might never return to it as Vice-President. In fact, even though Quadros had been fairly certain that Lott's fall would lead to him taking power, Lacerda and Adhemar's plotting made it such that even his ascension to the presidency was something of a surprise.

In the end, it mattered not. Quadros was now President; his first act upon entering the office that was now his was to order an aide to grab a disinfectant and a paper towel so he could clean up the chair.

The aide left, and Quadros fell into a reverie. All the moments in which that fool Lott had ignored his advice came to mind. When confronted with such folly, what choice did he have but to be better? He swore before God that he would be a better leader for Brazil than that wretched general ever could. The broom would sweep up the shards that the golden sword left in its fall.

When the assistant returned Quadros took the cleaning implements and immediately went to work on the office chair, not only cleaning the seat but its back and legs. A look of bemusement crossed the young bureaucrat's face. “What are you doing, sir? Why clean it again when the cleaners already took care of it?”

Quadros shook his head in dismissal, saying, “It has to be done.”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.1.a: “This chair is filthy - it has been infected by devious buttocks.”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.2.desc:
Lorenzo Moura thought of himself as a rational man. He worked hard, had a nice family, earnt a good wage and had respectable hobbies practised with his normal friends. Being such a man, despite his political ignorance, he knew that the only political party that could truly serve Brazil was the UDN, and that the others were all corrupt, incompetent, or socialists, facets that he loathed. Whenever he did learn of their failings, he couldn't help but feel angered.

BREAKING: HENRIQUE LOTT FOUND TAKING BRIBES IN BRASÍLIA

Moura saw red. He was always suspicious of Henrique Lott, and had heard some dire rumours about his corruption, but the detail that the article provided, explaining (not photographed only as Lott would've attacked the journalist) in a way practically insulting to the calm Moura, who couldn't help but shout in anger at the callous dishonesty of Lott, expecting to get away with such blatant abuse done in such a public manner.

HOW WEALTHY IS LOTT REALLY?

Moura was shocked. Lott was corrupt, sure, but he always at least painted himself as honest. This very article, though, clearly debunked that pervasive myth. It highlighted just how much of the funding for the Trans-Amazonian Highway had been syphoned off, paying for lavish parties at hidden mansions. Secretly, of course, Lott wasn't silly enough to party so openly. And yet, the press saw all.

LACERDA ANNOUNCES INVESTIGATION INTO MILITARY CORRUPTION

At long last, Moura felt soothed once again. The past few days had been a blur for him, as he could scarcely believe the increasingly damning reports coming in about Lott's lavish lifestyle and plentiful abuses as General, and as President. To hear that Lacerda had finally been pushed into investigation affirmed his belief. After all, who of such moral calibre wouldn't?
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.2.a: In the boardroom, the Crow cackled that his opponent's legacy lay destroyed
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.3.desc:
“God, how I need a drink,” Quadros muttered.

The source of his desire for alcohol this time around was the spending records of the previous Lott administration. As was the case whether or not Lott decided to take his sensible advice, the spending - especially on that asinine Trans-Amazonian highway to the tenth circle of hell - was always simply appalling. “It's all so tiresome, I tell you,” Quadros said to the aide handing him his papers.

Fortunately, Quadros thought, he could at least do something about this mess. Aside from slashing the spending on Lott's damn fool project, he could do something yet better to ensure there was no wrecking in response to his plans.

Quadros noted the names of the people mentioned as principals in the execution of the project, then connected them to a list he had of corrupt officials and businessmen involved in project-related graft. From here it would be relatively simple: if they did not comply with his directives to cut costs, he would simply reveal their corruption schemes to the Brazilian body politic.

As he started to write out the telegrams to the various officials he was about to threaten, he felt the irritation returning. So he issued an order to the attending assistant:
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.3.a: “For God's sake! Get me a bottle of strong whisky. What a thrice-damned awful project.”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.4.desc:
“Soldiers! By directive of the President of the Republic, we are now to withdraw to base and end our contribution to active combat. It is the sentiment of the Government and the Ministry that further involvement in the South African conflict is not opportune for us.”

Luizinho knew what that meant: that man Quadros was planning to bring the soldiers home. It was probably for the best, Luizinho thought; fighting was not something he wanted to make a lifetime job out of. Besides, it was good to have a chance to avoid adding to the nightmares he was already having.

A convoy of trucks came to his camp to pick him up and help dismantle his company's setup. Some American friends of the company had come by to bid farewell. Luizinho talked with his officer and convinced him to leave behind some useful odds and ends for them as thanks for their camaraderie.

In the end, Luizinho thought as he got into the truck and looked back, it was for the best. The Americans would hopefully be able to pick up the slack anyway.

But despite the upcoming joy of going home and never having to go through a battle again, he could not shake a feeling of guilt, or the fear that he was abandoning his American comrades.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.4.a: Such feelings were common throughout the withdrawing Brazilian forces.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.5.desc:
“Ladies, gentlemen, delegates of the Organization of Free Nations. Today, in accordance with the directives issued by Brasília and Itamaraty, I must inform you that due to a reevaluation of domestic priorities and the general situation within the Brazilian Republic, we cannot commit to regular attendance of OFN Council meetings at this time.”

At this point, the Brazilian ambassador to the United States visibly put down his speech paper. Knowledgeable people in the audience knew why that was: that maniac Quadros probably wanted the Ambassador to hurl insults at the OFN and the United States. Not only was that foolish, it was not a sentiment the ambassador shared.

The diplomat continued: “Reassessments of Brazilian priorities have played out in a manner many would legitimately deem unconventional, and the response thereto is certainly, shall we say, idiosyncratic and unique. However, I can make very clear Brazil's commitment to democracy, freedom, and the preservation of Brazilian-OFN cooperation to the maximum extent possible without compromising our national interests.”

On hearing that the Secretary of State, also in the audience for the day, smirked. Though Quadros was too much of an idiotic drunk to comprehend such veiled wordings, the Secretary understood what the good Ambassador was saying. “Ah well,” America's chief diplomat muttered.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.5.a: “At least some Brazilians are still sensible these days.”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.6.desc:
It was 10 a.m. in Brasília. For some reason, to the bemusement of the aide that went into the presidential office in the Planalto Palace, President Quadros was already well into his sixth caipirinha of the day. The aide's mouth opened to say something, but then he thought better of it and simply handed the document over.

“Sir, this is a report on an opposition congressman, a Pessedista, who is suspected of receiving bribes from national companies.” Quadros immediately sat up straight, or he would anyway if he was not rather... tired and emotional. “What?! You n-n-n-n-eed to shend the polishe in. The military! G-get that bashtard arreshted! At onshe!”

The assistant had feared the President would say that. He tried to get him to calm down: “Sir, that isn't how it works, we need to have an investigation by the pertinent authorities. If we just arrest him we'll get accused of abuse of power. Do you-”

“NO!” Quadros shouted, cutting him off. “You imbeshiles, we will d-do it my way! Now the two, no, four of yoush get the fuck out of here at onshe or I'lls have you all fired, by the Bleshed Virzhin!” There was only one aide in the office with Quadros.

Raising his hands placatingly, the aide quickly backed out for his own safety and to avoid getting fired. As he left the only thought in his head was...
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.6.a: “F-four of me? God, he really is drunk.”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.7.desc:
“As such, after days of thorough investigation inside presidential candidate Adhemar's mansion, the federal police have concluded that the governor has received no irregular money. The investigation has now been called off, and Adhemar has told us that he was never worried about anything and that-”

“What a bunch of buffoonery.” Quadros exclaimed as he furiously turned off the radio. “You're telling me that not a single cent inside that wretched safe is tainted? For the love of God, stop jesting!”

It was clear to the bespectacled President that putting down the bull would not be an easy task because now he has to fight the country's police force to successfully sweep away the evil that tainted the beautiful streets of São Paulo. Even a baby would know that Adhemar bribed the police officers to fend them off.

After adjusting his glasses and cleaning off his face, Quadros got up and waltzed off his office towards the phone lying on a table outside his office. On the other side of the phone was a man named Carvalho Pinto, the honorary President of MPJQ, Quadros's master plan to dominate Brazilian Politics.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.7.a: The time to rally the people has come.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.8.desc:
Jânio Quadros swaggered into the room where the economists in service to the Brazilian Government were conferring, dressed in a set of white slacks with matching white shoes more fit for a walk in the jungle than the uniform of the President. The economists looked at each other for a moment and silently agreed not to say anything about it; at least the man wasn't drunk.

Quadros took advantage of their silence to have the first word. “Gentlemen, you are aware that thanks to me the Brazilian economy is at last headed towards something resembling prosperity. My measures have successfully cut down on inflation, and the influence of those whoreson mountebanks in the PSD over our state-owned companies and our government is being reduced; surely you gentlemen agree that we are clearly on the right path.”

An economist spoke up in reply. “Yes, sir, your methods do in fact show promise, but there is one thing we want to recommend. We think it might further stabilize the economy if you sell some of the state companies' shares to private investors.”

At that the President went from cheerful to outraged. “What kind of Jacobinical, demoniacal, reprobate suggestion is that? Selling off the state companies to private investors?! Absolutely not! If I do something as inane as that, those stocks will fall into evil hands!”
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.8.a: The economists tried and failed to hide their worry.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.9.desc:
“PEOPLE OF BRAZIL!

In the recent days since the fall of the feckless general Lott from the Presidency and my ascension in his place, I have taken many important measures to protect the economy from the depredations of foreigners and corrupt men of the Establishment.

We have moved decisively and have successfully cut down on inflation, and the influence of the mountebanks that formed the previous administration over our state-owned companies and our government is being reduced. But the supporters of the old, degenerate, Godless order are not powerless.

Day after day in the National Congress and throughout the halls of power in Brazil, the congressmen and senators of this Republic, concerned only with themselves rather than the common welfare, have consistently sabotaged the measures proposed by my government.

Therefore I call upon you for your assistance in this crucial time. I ask you to pressure your elected representatives to listen to my counsel and save Brazil from disaster before it is too late.

J. QUADROS
PRESIDENT OF BRAZIL

This announcement was in a newspaper. Some people, mostly Jânists, went out and did as Quadros said. Others had only the following in reply:
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.100.desc:
Surrounded by the men of the recently-formed Movimento Popular Jânio Quadros, Quadros harangued an adoring crowd at a rally in São Paulo in the aftermath of the passage of the Anti-Restriction Act.

“Ladies and gentlemen, good Paulista citizens: this day, we have done a great thing! We have passed the Anti-Restriction Act!” The people applauded and screamed their approval, but Quadros kept talking over them.

“Yes, we have passed the Act, and with the grace of God we shall pass more still. There is still work to do, as you all know; I still have a crusade to fight within the halls of Brasília. The Godless infidels, enslaved to their own interests, will continue to chain Brazil to economic restrictions so they can fill their own pockets with money while the average Brazilian is devoured alive by inflation unless I am there to stop them!”

The crowd cheered. Meanwhile, two passerby economists from the local universities looked at each other in concern as Quadros continued to shout. One said to the other, “If he uses this little success of his to expand state-owned companies, I shudder to think about what will happen to the economy.”

The second economist sighed and shook his head.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.101.desc:
Quadros had failed a legislative project. His default coping mechanism in a case like this was to drink and drink hard while lolling about in his office chair in the Planalto. This time around his drink of choice was beer rather than caipirinha.

In his drunken rage, he began to curse people out that were not in the room with him. Campos and Lott were his most frequent targets. “That N-nazhifashshisht gommunisht Proteshtant atheisht whoreshun Gamposh, if he had just d-done his fuuucking duty and gotten enouf fucking votersh...”

Someone opened the door, but Quadros paid it no mind.

“And that fucking zheneral Lottie, if he'd, he'd, he'd not made thoshe motherfucking restrictionsh in the firsht place I wouldn't be having this damned problem... eh, w-w-what's thish?” Seven glasses of water connected to seven hands had emerged in front of his eyes. Quadros looked up and saw seven aides, who all looked the same.

The officials said, “Sir, might you take some water instead? This beer won't be any good for your health long term.”

“Rubbish-sh-sh-sh! N-nonshenshe! By the A-a-a-apareshida,”-here Quadros interrupted himself to gag-“water'zh only good fer, fer washing carsh! The seven, no, fifteen of you get the fuck out of my offishe!” Then he gagged again.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.101.a: The aide (there was only one) nodded sadly and quickly backed out of the office.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.200.desc:
The Anti-Trust Act passed amidst the applause of UDN members in the National Congress.

The President, his morale strengthened by this legislative tour de force, stood up and swaggered to the podium to make a speech. Of course, this being Quadros, the speech was pointlessly inflammatory and threatening - however, given it was the PSP being targeted, no one really cared other than PSP men.

“People of Brazil, members of the accursed PSP, pay close attention to my words.” Glaring at the PSP delegates, he continued. “Know that I am coming for your leader, to do away with his corrupt plague upon our land!” The UDN men applauded, the PSP men shouted their anger, and the rest simply left - this nonsense was beneath them.

Quadros was undeterred by their responses; he was in the zone. “Let God and Brazil serve as my witness - I will have that corrupt good-for-nothing rooting around in a stable from which he cannot escape, like the bull he claims he is!”

Hearing this remark, the UDN and PSP men outright started brawling, with the PSP getting the worst of it. Seeing that Quadros merely chuckled and left the podium.
strings.BRA_quadroshundreddays.201.desc:
“Yes. I need to speak to President Quadros at his earliest convenience.”

“I'll see what I can do, Governor Lacerda. Give me some time.”

The aide ran from the phone to the door of the Presidential office, where Jânio Quadros, having just failed to pass the Anti-Trust Act, was drowning his sorrows yet again. This time it was a mix of beer and caipirinha that Quadros made by dumping a glass of one into a glass of the other over and over.

“Sir, Carlos Lacerda wishes to speak to you at your earliest convenience.”

“W-W-WHAT? That c-crow fucker of a parabolic funcshion? That motherfucking logarithm?! Get him out! I don't want him anywhere near my fucking offishe! Get out of here too, the three of you!”

Once again marvelling at how Quadros managed to see more than one of him every time he got drunk, the aide went back to the phone. “I'm sorry, sir, but the President is unavailable and I can't indicate when he can speak to you today.”

There was a few seconds' silence. “... Duly noted.”

Lacerda, on hanging up, was furious. Was that drunken son of a whore going to mess everything up left, right, and centre and allow this country to fall into the hands of the Varguists again? He picked the phone up and began to place calls to the offices of various UDN delegates he knew were in the office. If Quadros would not do his job, then Lacerda would build an opposition within the alliance to throw Quadros out and keep the presidency in UDN hands.
strings.BRA_denys.1.desc:
Odílio Denys carefully caressed his brow with a grayish handkerchief, the sweat accumulated causing his mind to fumble and his thoughts to worry. Though his worries were, in truth, pure and real, as he sat witness to the members of his National Defense bloc. A copy of an extract, taken from a leaked version of the Lott act, rested before each member as they flicked through the pages liberally, at their own paces.

“It most likely has the numbers to pass,” Denys spoke, a calm mask hiding his true feelings of immediate dread. The awe of his peers were nearly comical, their faces tense and shocked in juxtaposition to the speaker, “And in turn, we most likely have to unite our forces to ensure its defeat.”

Though the loyalties of the men before him were already in much different places. Some stood and left without a word, others bowed in respect and rushed out, with a minority remaining behind to aid Denys in his ventures, “The madness of the Act must be halted at once, good men.”

Being addressed, the only remainders of the NDC bobbed their heads in assent, nodding frivolously as they listened to the words of Denys, “All diplomacy with Lott has failed. All negotiations have failed. It is now up to us to end this madness and return Brazil to the order it desperately needs.”
strings.BRA_denys.1.a: An end to the Mad King?
strings.BRA_denys.2.desc:
The phone rang repeatedly around Costa e Silva's office, the cacophony of sounds tormenting the man as he finally reached to answer whichever caller he had received. He little expected a familiar voice to respond on the other end, that which he immediately recognized to belong to Denys, who croaked in a hushed yet stern tone.

“Hello, Silva,” began Denys all the way on his other end, close enough to the microphone to hear his rushed breath, “I have some very particular news. The madness of the Lott Act is soon to find itself within the Senate, and to be voted on. This simply cannot occur, if you understand what I mean.”

“I understand,” Silva replied nearly immediately, now standing from his seat and rushing to his office desk, “You can expect my complete loyalty, Senhor Denys, I can assure you that I will join your endeavors should they... come to such. In fact, I will contact Olímpio Filho, I am certain that he will do much the same to aid you.”

“Thank you, Silva,” Denys hushed, his face lit up by the given enthusiasm of the receiving end, “Without the military shuffled about in Brazil, our organizational advantage ensures our superiority should things go to worse. I would say that luck is on our side.”
strings.BRA_denys.2.a: “Not only luck is on our side, Senhor Denys.”
strings.BRA_denys.3.desc:
Denys made a plethora of phone calls when the time had come appropriate, on that wretched day. First was the obvious, launching his most anticipated coup by ordering the Armed Forces to march into Brasília, all the while those loyal in his retinue marched to maintain order in other major cities.

In São Paulo his men acted with little resistance, while in Rio the city had already sworn its fealty to Denys with Olímpio Filho's fealty in control. Soon enough, all of Brazil would be under Denys, and the NDC continued to debate endlessly whether to support one or the other, blind to the gravity of the issue at hand.

Lott, in his stead, appeared live before a retinue of sergeants and soldiers, grunts and officers alike, of which he saw only a united force of plausible loyalists, “The day has come, fellow men,” he began, addressing all present, “The day to rally in defense of our proud nation. Treacherous commanders have seen it fit to declare our efforts unfit, and it is up to me, and you, to take up arms and fight for what we know is best.”
strings.BRA_denys.4.desc:
Along a highway to Brasília, a column of grim and nervous soldiers march towards the capital under the orders of Denys and his fellow plotters to remove their own President from power. The only thing standing between them and the strangling of Brazilian democracy is a blockade defended by a line of equally grim yet determined military sergeants loyal to the President. From the marchers steps forward a young soldier, his boyish face contorted into a grimace, shouting, “Lay down your arms and disperse! We have been given orders from Marshal Denys himself; for the sake of national security, congress must remove President Lott from office!” His opposition remained unmoved. “Last chance! Disarm and disperse!” at the soldier's warning, one of the sergeant's eyes narrowed and he broke from his ranks, striding towards his counterpart with an expression of barely contained fury “Drop your gun!” he cried as sweat poured down his face, but the sergeant continued until he was within arms reach “I said drop-”

His sentence was cut short as the sergeant's open palm struck him across the face. “You scum took an oath! You vowed to defend the republic and the people!” He ranted, uncaring for the rifles trained on him. “You promised to protect the people from tyrants and now you're marching on behalf of one! If any of you have any shred of dignity and duty left in your souls, turn your asses around and go home!” For a moment, there was silence.

Then, one by one, the marcher's faces turned shameful and they turned back, their wills broken. Similar incidents would follow across the country, as unmotivated and uncertain pro-coup forces, unwilling to turn their weapons on their comrades in arms, were turned back in the face of more determined loyalists. The NDC would not sit idle as the coup fell to pieces, and swiftly turned on Denys, ordering their men to join the loyalists in defense of Lott and arrest the plotters. Marshal Denys ranted and raved in the face of his failure in the scant few hours of freedom he had left, before being taken and imprisoned by his own men.
strings.BRA_denys.4.a: The courage of few have beaten the wrath of the many.
strings.BRA_denys.5.desc:
As Lott entered the room, all he could hear was silence. The officers of the National Defense Council stared at him in expectation, their faces inexpressive, boring into him like drills. Turning his eyes away from them, he began his speech.

“Gentlemen, these last few days have been hard, for the military and Brazilian democracy. Once again, a bunch of rogues thought they could seize the government away from the people, and again, they failed. Thanks to your efforts, the will of the people lives another day, and for that they shall be ever grateful. While some in the military stood against us, I am proud to see that so many of you stayed loyal. That, I believe, is a testament to the Brazilian military spirit.

It is a hard thing to recognise that the traitors were once our comrades, but this is the hard truth. Can we be give mercy to this kind of dissent? No, to give them but a slap on the wrist would do nothing but embolden this behaviour, and allow our country to edge closer to a devastating conflict. They shall be stripped of their ranks, kicked out of the army, never to return. Yet their fates, I leave to you gentlemen. I trust you to be fair and just, and to give them the sentences they deserve.”

Lott gazed around, hoping to see approval. The NDC responded with a small round of applause and smiles abound. None of them seemed particularly enthusiastic about the idea, but at least there was no immediately visible sign of revolt. He sighed with relief; while the military was not yet pacified, not fully, they had at last been brought to heel. Brazilian democracy could breathe easier now, or at least until the next ambitious general came around.
strings.BRA_denys.5.a: Whatever happens, democracy had protectors now.
strings.BRA_denys.6.desc:
Only a few officers and soldiers had rallied behind the cause of Lott. The NDC had finally deemed it fit to exit its bureaucratic loopholes and deem him unconstitutional and dangerous for the integrity of Brazil. They even went as far as to request his resignation, for the sake of avoiding further damage.

Henrique Lott was having none of it. In his most desperate appeal, he held out and make a rushed call to the American embassy in seek of the ambassador's help, “Please, Gordon,” Lott made his plead, “It is pertinent to have the American's help during these times of trial, so that this may not spiral out of control!”

Gordon scratched his brow as he pondered, holding the phone close to his face in what must have been an eternal silence for either man on either side. As the seconds become minutes, he finally volunteered to break the ice and speak his truth, though he did not personally adore it; “I will see what I can do, and I will contact as many as must to ensure your survival...”
strings.BRA_denys.7.desc:
Lott tapped his fingers together lightly, in admitted terror of what might occur next with most anticipation. He waited eagerly, by the phone, staring at the complexity of the artifact to ease his mind of the horrors that ensued. Though they had already occurred. His blank stare now took to face the window, taking but a few steps to stare down at the land below.

In files, coupists stood hand by hand surrounding his abode, all clad in his nation's uniform with the banners associated with it. It all occurred extremely quickly, the situation flying by as it was properly explained and laid down to him by some Denys man.

The officer spoke about the surrounding of Congress, and how Auro Andrade had personally stamped a law removing Lott as President. Lott had no time to think, as he opened his lips only to say “I resign,” no man being able to gain the satisfaction of ending his presidency.

The newly appointed interim leader of Brazil later in the evening received a phone call of his own, from a very unexpected source, “Lott must be ensured a light sentence. It would be ridiculous on both our nations should he die.” Denys agreed. He hung the phone, staring out his own window into the streets of Brasília, as the men and women of the nation eagerly waited for the next election cycle and a rebirth of Brazil.
strings.BRA_denys.7.a: An end to the Mad King.
strings.BRA_denys.8.desc:
“That fucking bastard!”

“Treasonous little shit, no wonder he wanted us out of the way!”

Denys watched the gathering of generals before him vent their outrage with grim satisfaction. In hindsight, the treacherous nature of the President had been evident long ago; his close cooperation with leftists, his open Varguism, his disrespect for his own military's high command, and now an act to vandalize the constitution. But the man was going to reap what he sowed, men that had lost what they had rightfully earned, like Olímpio Mourão Filho and Sílvio Frota, had come together to take a stand, and now he just needed to get them on track.

“Gentlemen.” His stern tone silenced the seething murmurs and angry shouts and brought attention back to himself. “We are all rightfully furious and disgusted, but we must also be precise and decisive. To say the destiny of Brazil lies in our hands would be putting it lightly, and as such, I have devised a plan that will save our nation from the President's betrayal.”

“Within two weeks from now, we will hear radios across the country play the FIFA World Cup's anthem, but this will be cut off roughly a minute in and instead begin to play our national anthem. This will be your signal to mobilize the men under our command and march on the nearest cities, along with any other location of strategic importance.”

“Now, I want to emphasize this: our goal is to force Lott's resignation or to cut ties with leftists and end his Act before it can begin. We will accomplish this by making either him or congress see reason or through intimidation. This will not be easy; Lott has fortified himself with generals loyal to him. We must expect resistance.”

“Finally, remember that this is a coup to save democracy and not a bloodbath! Avoid violence wherever you can, and remember that, if we must, we will remove the President, but he must not be harmed!” Some of the generals looked nervous, but the determination was there, which was all he needed. “Now, go back to your men and be ready for further instruction for our signal. God save Brazil!”
strings.BRA_denys.8.a: The cheers of generals drown out the sobbing of liberty.
strings.BRA_denys.9.desc:
“-and that is why I need your help. If we are to succeed in ending President Lott's attempt to defile our constitution and threaten national security, then we need you and your men to ensure we will take São Paulo.” Marshal Denys finished his plea to Second Army's commander General Kruel with a clenched fist. The fate of Brazil was in dire straits, and the man he sought help from remained unmoved, in a lazy slouch in his seat with an alcoholic drink in one hand, and an amused smirk etched on his face.

“Oh, I don't know.” Denys had to resist the urge to scream at the man. “My experience with our dear President has left me with the impression that he has a good head on his shoulders and is wise in judgment.” Kruel rose slightly from his slouch to sit up straight. “I cannot help but wonder what I could gain from turning against him.” There was a glint in the man's eyes now, dangerous and greedy.

“I see.” So that was what the fate of Brazil was going to come to. A greedy fuck looking for a bribe.

“The task ahead is expected to be costly and stressful, and we will be more than ready to... compensate you for whatever monetary and material costs this may require of you. And, of course, your actions to safeguard Brazil will be recognized as qualities of a man who deserves a higher station. Tell me, how does the name 'Minister of Defense Amaury Kruel' sound to you?” The man smiled in satisfaction.
strings.BRA_denys.10.desc:
“-and that about sums up what is needed.” Denys finished his sentence with a short nod to General Amaury Kruel. Convincing him to go along with the coup plot was easy. The man had felt slighted by Lott when he was passed over for commander of the São Paulo forces and was eager to hit back. For a price, of course.

Even so, Denys could not help but feel anxious. The army around the city was staffed with Lott loyalists, and it was doubtful they would fold over to Kruel and his men. And then he would have to take the rest of the state as well...

His uncertainty must have shown on his face because Kruel's morphed into a scowl. “What, you think me and my men can't pull this off?” He stared into Denys' eyes with fury before his face twisted into a sneer. “Don't worry, I'll have Brizola and Bevilacqua under control when the time comes; just get my fucking money ready until then.” Denys gave the man another nod before walking out of his office, but his fears lingered.
strings.BRA_denys.10.a: “I hope so, Kruel, I hope so...”
strings.BRA_denys.11.desc:
The soldiers received the signal, and as tasked, acted immediately. In tremendous swiftness, Olímpio Filho succeeded in leading his troops to move into Rio, to link up with Carlos Lacerda who waited idly wherever he may be. Little did the men know, that they had just jumped the gun.

Lott, in his stead, awoke in the rush of being shaken around aggressively by Assis Brasil in a most spontaneous fashion. He would have ignored him, though the face of confusion upon his peer was most telling of the importance, “What is it?”

“Men have marched into Rio, though what seems to be prematurely. Somewhat disorganized,” he gave a cough, squinting and frotting his eyes. Lott then queried; “Where is Denys? Do we know of his whereabouts?”

“I do not know,” muttered Assis Brasil in response, shrugging profusely. Lott then spoke up again, practically interrupting him, “Bring me General Jair Dantas Ribeiro, we must crush this coup while we have enough time to prepare an assault on Brasília.”

“And what of you, Senhor Lott?” wondered Assis Brasil, halfway out the room in the same rush as anyone in that early morning “Should you not seek somewhere more secure? Should bad come to worse...”
strings.BRA_denys.12.t: It Has to Be This Way
strings.BRA_denys.12.desc:
President Henrique Teixeira Lott's office was in a flurry of panicked activity. One moment the country enjoyed the sound of the FIFA anthem then cut to its national anthem, and it all went to hell. His worst fears were coming to pass; military units were marching on cities and army bases to seize control of the surrounding territories, demanding his resignation across the country. And it seemed that Denys was missing. Lott had a gut feeling he knew what his marshal was up to, which left a sinking feeling in his gut.

“Sir!” one of his secretaries yelled to him with a frightened expression from their phone. “It's Denys.” Lott strode towards the trembling man, took the phone from their shaking arm, and steeled himself.

“I'm here, Denys. Let's get this over with.”

“President Lott, I want you to know that we only do this to preserve the constitution of Brazil and its stability.” Lott had suspected Denys was involved in the coup, but it didn't soften the blow. Denys continued. “We demand the end of the collaboration between your government. Any left-wing ministers will be removed immediately. After this, we expect you to rule over a unity government until the next election. Finally, we demand the constitution be protected: the Lott Act must be destroyed.” Lott took in a deep, shuddering breath before speaking.

“You want me to be nothing but a decorative President. I refuse, on all accounts.”

“Henrique-”

“Marshal, I don't abandon my friends. If you want to be rid of me so badly, then step out of the shadows, put your men on the street, and betray me publicly.” The line went dead. A mere hour later, the President would learn that Denys' men were attempting to surround Brasília.
strings.BRA_denys.13.desc:
Lott felt like he had aged fifty years in five hours. Since the start of the coup, he and his staff had spent the day frantically calling up every governor and general they could to rally in defense of the President and democracy. First, it had just been the likes of the governor of Goiás and generals like Brasils but as the day dragged on, so did the calls, and all remained uncertain.

One of his secretaries suddenly rose from their chair while on the phone and turned to him, “Sir! It's the Rio forces. The man on the line says the coup forces gave up!”

Lott rushed over to the man and took the phone with a silent thanks. “This is President Lott. What's happened?”

“Mr. President, this is General Ribeiro of the Rio de Janeiro forces” the general spoke with a stern but relieved tone, “the traitors led by Mourão attempted to march on the city. I responded by getting all my tanks together on the roads and daring the bastards to try it. They folded.”

“I see, thank you. Thank you.” The general hummed in acknowledgment before barking something at one of his men and hanging up. Lott felt relief flood his form and grinned. “Gentlemen!” his voice brought all attention in the room to him. “The situation is still dire, but we are winning! If the coup d'etat forces cannot take the major cities, they have already failed, tell our men to keep it up, and we will prevail!” The room exploded into cheers, and the men faced their duties with renewed vigor.
strings.BRA_denys.13.a: Brazil prevails over its darkest hour.
strings.BRA_denys.14.desc:
Henrique Lott took a moment to reflect. The coup was nearing its end, and he had won. It was ironic, really. This coup was born in response to an act to curtail the power and influence of the military. But all it had done was validate every concern he had. Was it all so important to them? Was what he was planning such an insult to them that they would instead use brute force than diplomacy? Was there ever a time he could have made them see reason and avoid this mess?

His reflection was cut short when a secretary waved him over with one hand and a phone in the other. Lott moved with a grateful smile and took the phone. “Hello, this is President Lott. To whom am I speaking?”

“Ah, my President! General Kruel speaking.” he heard a murmur in Kruel's background. “Oh, and General Frota is here too. But! More importantly, we have a third guest!” Lott began to feel his patience with the man wearing thin, drumming free fingers along a nearby desk. Before he could tell them to get on with it, the General spoke again, “We have captured the traitorous Marshal Denys! Hey, bastard, why don't you say something?” A moment later, he could make out more sound from Kruel's background; this time, it was a chorus of swears and threats before it was silenced.

“Well, it certainly does sound like him.” Lott wondered if this was a part of some bizarre, hair-brained plot before dismissing the thought. While it was rather suspicious that these two men somehow found the rogue marshal before anyone and apprehended him, it was more prudent to deal with Denys now, and the rest could wait. “My thanks, generals. Do you need assistance in his transportation?”
strings.BRA_denys.14.a: Brazilian democracy has been tested, and not found wanting.
strings.BRA_denys.15.desc:
As Lott stared down his old friend through the prison bars, that was the only question he had. “What the hell led you - who stood behind us the whole way in 1955 - to betray your oath to the State and democracy, to stab me of all people in the back like this?”

Odílio Denys had only one response. “It had to be done, Henrique. It had to be done. Your law was unconstitutional.”

“What, and your little coup against a duly elected government wasn't? What do you take me for, a Lacerdista?”

Denys scoffed. “I took you for someone enslaved to the Trabalhista communists, and you've proven me right. Mark my words, if you let that Brizola come anywhere near power we'll all be singing the praises of Hitler or Lenin before long. We won't be able to fight communism or fascism, not with the Supreme Court defending your law thanks to our failure.”

The marshal outside the prison cell shook his head. “No, Denys. We will fight fascism and communism perfectly fine with the Lott Act in place. As for you, you should not speak; you are just a traitor who betrayed his oaths.”

“I-”

The President of the United States of Brazil turned away.

“I have nothing more to say to you.”
strings.BRA_denys.15.a: They never spoke to each other again.
strings.BRA_denys.16.t: The Best Laid Plans of Mice and Men
strings.BRA_denys.16.desc:
“Rio has been taken!”

“That fucker Kruel betrayed us!”

“Aragão is too far out at sea; he can't help us.”

The reports kept coming in and out, but Lott wasn't paying attention. A severe numbness overtook his entire being, drowning out all around him. He had lost. The coup had gathered too many generals for him to defeat. And those loyal to him were too few or too sluggish. Where did it all go wrong? Had he not done enough to ensure the military's loyalty? Pushed too far? Not gone far enough? What were they going to do when they got rid of him?

“Sir.” A crestfallen man with a phone called to him. “It's your daughter.”

That snapped him out of his depression, and he hurried to accept the phone with a trembling hand. “Edna? Are you safe?”

“I should be asking you that!” He'd never heard her so frightened before. “Father, please, I know what's happening. You need to run, find a car, a plane, anything. Just get out of the country!”

The President exhaled with an exhausted sigh. “I can't do that. I have my duty.”

“To hell with your duty! And your pride, what about your life?” Her voice began to break. “If they catch you they, they-”

“Edna.” He mustered as much confidence as he could. “They won't kill me. Denys won't let them.” Truth be told, he wasn't sure about that. He'd made a poor judge of Denys' character already. “Edna? No matter what happens, I want you to know that I am proud of you. Goodbye.”

“Father-” Lott cut the line.
strings.BRA_denys.17.desc:
Henrique Lott stared at the distant outskirts of Brasília atop the Presidential palace, and although he was grasping his binoculars it was clear to him that even a man blind in one eye could see the troops massing outside the capital. He stared at the gathering army blankly and without any real thoughts on his mind; it was strangely calming, the noise of radio chatter and his bodyguards talking to him drowned out by the realization of his situation. It all felt... cathartic somehow to Lott, but his wandering mind would soon be caught by one of his bodyguards shaking his shoulder and yelling at him.

“Sir! Mr. President!” The man shouted, holding a walkie talkie by his ear. “We've gotten word from several states that they're willing to commit troops in support of us, and that you just need to give the order.”

Lott pulled a pack of cigarettes and his lighter from within his pocket and lit it before turning to the guard. “I don't want to tear this country apart more than it already has. I've already lost, there's nothing more I or anyone else can do without causing more unnecessary damage.” He paused, taking a deep drag from the cigarette. “Give me the radio, I'll talk to Odílio myself.” The guardsman reluctantly handed Lott the radio, turning away to leave and inform the others of Lott's decision. As the man left, Lott took a deep breath and started speaking. “Odílio, you win. I won't put up a fight, come get me here and let's just get this over with.”

“What? Just like that?” A confused voice boomed through the radio, Denys was taken aback by Lott's decision; he had expected a much stiffer resistance from a man of Lott's standing. “Yes, just like that Odílio. Now get this goddamn knife out of my back and just kill me already.” Lott angrily quipped. Whatever reply Denys had about holding elections to deal with the chaos he had caused was lost to Lott, having lowered the radio as his mind began to wander again and he looked out once more to the distant army that had been assembled against him. In his mind, there was but one single quote:
strings.BRA_denys.17.a: “O Deus, do not forget who has caused all these woes.”
strings.BRA_lacerda.16.desc:
When the senators of the UDN coalition were asked to attend an impromptu meeting at the personal request of President Carlos Lacerda, they went along with haste, eager to see what he had in store.

“My partymen,” he began, “my senators, my countrymen. Brazil has been lying in wait for a better future, and I have arrived to deliver it. I am proud to have served my country well! The economy has been improved, and political instability decreased. The road is brighter than before!” The senators applauded, and not just out of responsibility; his oration was genuinely powerful.

“Thank you, my men, and thank you, to the people of Brazil, to all that you have done. I am glad that you have elected me to another term!” Murmurs. To so brazenly, openly and publicly rally against the official result; it would cause controversy, and the crowd was uneasy. “My next term comes, and it will deliver even more change! The legacy of Vargas, and all those who support him, will be removed; the stain of Getulism will no longer poison Brazil! Tyranny will be slain!” An audible silence, a gap in breath; not a soul in the room would dare question the man's words.

Wordlessly, some senators stood, turning to leave the chamber, backs towards Lacerda. But then, of those who remained, a vanguard began to clap. A standing ovation, which the rest joined in, until all left in the chamber formed a powerful crowd.

It matters not that some left, Lacerda thought. It matters that most stayed.
strings.BRA_lacerda.16.a: “I am the President, and the Senado serves me.”
strings.BRA_lacerda.0.desc:
Like a man at the casino, like a schoolboy waiting for his test scores, like a young man waiting for a response from his love; the anticipation of what's to come, the uncertain results of an important event left Lacerda nervous, able to feel his heart pounding in his chest.

And then it happened. The polls were closed, the votes were tallied, and the numbers were on the television. Lacerda had lost.

The votes had not yet all been counted, but over 90% had, and Lacerda could win a supermajority of the remaining votes and still not win. The election had been lost, it had been settled, and it was clear that Lacerda was defeated. Defeated by a Getulist, a leftist, a fucking crypto-communist! What in hell, what in the FUCK happened?

No. This couldn't be real. Goulart cheated, of course he did! He stuffed the ballots, he burned the real ones, he bribed the election officials. Brazil's a big country but not big enough to have enough brain-dead idiots that could be fooled into voting for someone as dangerous as Goulart. And he thinks he can get away with it! What a crock of shit!

Carlos sipped his drink. Some alcohol to cool his nerves. He can't get carried away like that, especially considering the trials to come, and what must be done. He looked at the calendar, saw how much time he'd have; about 80 days to inauguration - more precisely 78. Less than 80 days to reverse the fraud. Less than 80 days to save his country.

More alcohol to calm his nerves, but not enough to dull his wit. It's time to draft a plan. It was time for Lacerda to make arrangements and preparations for what must be done.
strings.BRA_lacerda.0.a: It's time to plan a coup.
strings.BRA_lacerda.1.desc:
The days were ticking. Goulart's inauguration was approaching; at least, that's what was thought. In this country, things like the presidency aren't decided on election day; they're decided between election day and inauguration, and it wouldn't be certain until Goulart was in the office; hell, even then it wasn't sure.

Lacerda was sitting by the window of the Palácio da Alvorada, admiring the view. Another beautiful sunset; the red filled the skies, the colors blended, and it was a gorgeous display of all beauty nature had to offer. But it was one day closer to the deadline, to his last days in the palace.

But he wasn't scared. He was already ready enough. The coup would go smoothly.

Carlos Lacerda thumbed through his notes, one by one. Population centers that needed to be seized. Critical figures in the military, those who were a good enough combination of bribable and powerful to be worth getting to his side. People who would support him even without greased palms. He had moved from a house of cards to a house of brick; it'll take a hell of a lot more than some breath, some talking, to take down what he's built up. And it was ready to go.

One name caught Lacerda's eyes in this final review. Frota, his trusted middleman, who had already proven well in advancing Lacerda's goals. It was time for him to do a great favor to Lacerda. It was time to talk with the military, and get the guns on his side.
strings.BRA_lacerda.1.b: Perhaps he had had too much to drink...
strings.BRA_lacerda.2.desc:
OPERATION PHOENIX

[?global.date.GetDateStringNoHour]

FOR APPROVED EYES ONLY

Upon the poor showings in the recent elections, it has been decided by Carlos Lacerda that drastic actions have been made necessary for the purpose of preserving and/or bettering the current situation within the state of Brazil.

Through phone calls, intermediaries, and other dispatch methods, contact has been made with several crucial figures to both the function and transition of the government. This includes high-up civilian and military officials. The state apparatus of Brazil has been sufficiently swayed to Lacerda's side for a restoration of proper, legitimate governance to be possible without overwhelming backlash.

Through de jure backing from politicians, and de facto backing from military officials, backed by soldiers loyal to them, a prevention of the inauguration of Goulart as President of Brazil will be executed. Major civilian centers, namely cities important to industry, trade and government, will be intervened in and held by military forces, ensuring important localities will be under Lacerda loyalist control.

This plan is now in effect.

SIGNED BY CARLOS LACERDA
strings.BRA_lacerda.3.desc:
Officers in the Brazilian Armed Forces have recently been rallying behind and declaring full allegiance to Carlos Lacerda, despite his loss to João Goulart in the recent elections held to determine President of the Republic. Called a coup by many, this has indicated a loss of stability and non-peaceful transfer of power in the state.

Marshal Amaury Kruel has declared allegiance to Lacerda, and has used his troops to seize the city of Brasília, placing the important governmental center under full military control. The result has been both a significant on-the-ground strengthening of Lacerdan forces, swaying the power struggle to his side, and a “falling in line effect” on the other generals of the Brazilian military, who see the way that the wind is blowing, and have decided to be on the side with plenty of guns.

Barricades have been placed in streets, nightly patrols are sweeping neighborhoods, and curfews have been put in effect, as the military is making sure of their control of their cities.

In an office, somewhere deep in friendly territory, Carlos Lacerda sits behind a desk, looking at Olímpio Mourão Filho, an important general. He stands at attention, shoulders broad, eyes filled with the respect a soldier is obliged to his Commander-in-Chief. There, in the dark room, Lacerda delivers an order.
strings.BRA_lacerda.3.a: “Filho, your job is to seize Guanabara.”
strings.BRA_lacerda.3.b: “Filho, your job is to seize Guanabara.”
strings.BRA_lacerda.4.desc:
The night began with various large moves being made by the Brazilian military, with some officers taking the initiative to seize various population centers in the name of Lacerda. However, the amount of pro-Lacerda officers has proven to not be enough to properly seize control of the country; the most important cities and resource centers have all stayed in government hands.

Teixeira Lott gives a speech, a great number of officers listening. In it, he tells officers to stay loyal, to the State, to the Constitution, it makes no difference; what matters is to not fall into the Lacerda camp. His words, or perhaps his reputation preceding him, was persuasive enough, and the officers fell into line, and a great deal of the pool of power that Lacerda drew from was completely neutralized, remaining loyal and aligned to the Constitutionalists. The officers side with the state.

Amury Kruel, a key ally of Lacerda, one of the initial supportive figures of the coup, is packing his bags. This wasn't just cowardice, though that may have played a role. It was made clear by the Constitutionalist figures that he was a threat, and it was also made clear that killing him would not be necessary, if he chose to accept a nice sum of money and a permanent vacation outside of Brazil. Naturally, he accepted, bringing with him Lacerda's hopes of a successful coup.
strings.BRA_lacerda.4.a: If failure is not a lesson, it is indeed a failure.
strings.BRA_lacerda.5.desc:
Ring, ring, ring. Domestic allies were not the only way to come to power here. The Americans had a finger in everything south of their border, and sooner or later they would take a stand; preferably one that favored Lacerda and his allies. He would contact the Americans, especially their military brass; he hoped his enemies had not already contacted them.

“Carlos Lacerda? I hear election night didn't go well for you. What do you need?”

“Well, you have two choices; the Brazilian people had two choices, too, but they chose wrong, of course. You can have Goulart or you can have me. And I promise you I'm much better for American interests.”

“Isn't it all about how good you are, how likely you are to win? We don't throw away American boys unless we get a promise of victory.”

“I have officers, I have legitimacy, I have military and civilian allies, I have control of population centers. You know the coup business, I know you know how this works. I know this is music to your ears.”

Silence for a moment. Probably a mute while the other military men were consulted, or they were calling Washington. Then an answer.
strings.BRA_lacerda.7.desc:
So far, so good. The military were keeping order, and the press were in lockstep. Order had come, and progress would soon follow. Brazil would be free of demagogues soon. However, the transition towards honest democracy could not be left purely to soldiers and journalists, and certainly not through his pen in Brasília. He had a lot of phone calls to make. A federal republic, as Lacerda's predecessors had wisely created, required federal support, or at least federal disinterest to ensure legitimacy. Even from those the central leadership considered otherwise... undesirable.

Take for example, the honourable governor of São Paulo and spawn of Lacerda's nemesis, Getúlio Vargas Filho. First as tragedy, then as farce, an old, hated voice chimed in. The son was just as much of a bastard and a kleptocrat as the father, though without his admittedly exceptional skill. Still, any imbecile could pose a threat when they also happen to be in charge of one of the most powerful territories in the nation. Doubly so if they believe themselves to have a mandate from the great Brazilian people, a fraudulent election, or the cult of Papa. Concessions would have to be negotiated. Through gritted teeth, perhaps, but negotiations all the same. He might refuse, but Vargas Junior would have the option of Lacerda or the military to negotiate with. Somehow, he doubted the military would offer a better deal.

The number was dialled, and after a few seconds, the governor of São Paulo picked up.
strings.BRA_lacerda.7.a: “Governor Vargas, I know we've had our differences...”
strings.BRA_lacerda.7.b: “Governor Vargas, I know we've had our differences...”
strings.BRA_lacerda.8.desc:
“What do you fucking mean, the military have joined the protests?” Lacerda bellowed at Ester. “The Paulistas are one thing, but in Guanabara of all places? Has the whole damned country gone insane?”

“Sir, I confirmed the reports are accurate myself. We cannot-”

“Shut up! Shut the fuck up! I need to think!” screamed Lacerda. How could this have happened? After so many years, he had finally come close to ridding Brazil of its taint. Vargas was rotting away in a wheelchair, his successor had been outmaneuvered, and the nation was finally on its way to sensible leadership. But no, old Getúlio had to haunt him from beyond the fucking grave with that waste of sperm son of his. He had been reasonable, he had been polite. He had been hung up on in five seconds, and blasted as a traitor on the radio within five minutes. Him? Called a traitor, an American puppet, a military stooge? By this waste of sperm of the man who had confined Brazil to a savage, dependent wasteland bereaved of talent, culture and honesty?

And it seemed the gallant people of Brazil stood behind the bastard. The ungrateful, cloying, useless wastes of a public body! After all he had done to free the land from despotism, a struggle which had continued for decades, but no, the people wanted to laze around on the back of the state, all the while blaming America for their insolence and their indolence! Fuck this. Fuck Brazil. Lacerda was done trying to help people who clearly did not want to help themselves. Let them rot in this stinking pit of human refuse. He stared around the office of the President one last time, thinking of all that could have been in a better world, before instructing Ester to have a helicopter prepared immediately.
strings.BRA_lacerda.8.a: A profound defeat for common sense.
strings.BRA_lacerda.9.desc:
Lacerda's meeting with the press executives had gone well, and they were ready to support a unified message to the Brazilian people. That was the easy part. Now he had to sit down, and use his calming words to extinguish any flames of insurrection from Goulart's supporters. He was somewhat apprehensive, his manner of speaking not well-adapted to the oratory flourishes and high rhetoric of his predecessors. But perhaps that was for the best. An era without strongmen or demagogues could not begin with a speech emulating the hollow promises of a past Lacerda sought to end. A reasonable tone for the speech would set a reasonable tone for the national mood. He began;

“Citizens of Brazil, this is your President speaking. It is my severe displeasure to inform the public of a series of disturbing revelations concerning irregularities which occurred the recent election. The full details have already been made available to the press, and will be published by tomorrow morning. For the time being, it is sufficient to say that allegations of voter intimidation, miscounting, and other impediments to the democratic process are credible and overwhelming. Thus, it is the solemn duty of the Brazilian government to annul the recent election results...”
strings.BRA_lacerda.9.a: “...until a full enquiry can be made...”
strings.BRA_lacerda.9.b: “...until a full enquiry can be made...”
strings.BRA_lacerda.10.desc:
Lacerda has been attempting to cast doubt on the election, accusing Goulart of many crimes, such as fraud and corruption, and the usual slew of insults that go from a loser to a winner. The intent of Lacerda has been, of course, to give people doubts about the legitimacy of the election, to give him an excuse to seize power back, aided by his various allies, domestic and foreign. Of course, this was predicated on one important thing; people believing him.

And people didn't believe him. His doubts were perceived, perhaps correctly, as just a last-ditch attempt to try and keep control of Brazil, and it failed. This has lead to a very undesirable position in Brazil, where two very high profile politicians are both claiming to be the rightful leader of the nation. However, it could be worse; Goulart's clear advantage, and the massive rallies and crowds behind him, paired with his legitimacy through the election, have given him enough power to, at least for now, avoid a civil war; but this may not last forever, and success is far from guaranteed.

Instability rising, and failures mounting, Lacerda is not in a good place at the moment. But he wanted power. He didn't want Brazil to burn. Faced with a loss, he will carry it with him, over the plains and over the oceans, to flee to a far-away place, a place with less failures for him. His past attempts be what they may, he doesn't wish to destroy the country.
strings.BRA_lacerda.11.desc:
Lacerda has been attempting to cast doubt on the election, accusing Goulart of many crimes, such as fraud and corruption, and the usual slew of insults that go around in a contested election. The intent of Lacerda has been, of course, to make the election seem illegitimate in the eyes of the people; and, for the purpose of this goal, he has succeeded.

It is not simply that everybody overnight has switched from voting for Goulart to voting for Lacerda; Lacerda does not need the die-hard support of the populace to have control of Brazil, as that's what the military's for. No. What Lacerda needs is for there to be enough doubt that the people will stay home, confused, worried, and, most importantly of all, far away from any Goulart rally. And this has been exactly what has happened; despite calls about a coup going on, and pleas to defend democracy, the people have stayed home, out of pro-Lacerda sympathies, out of fear, out of apathy, but they're home.

Lacerda sits back in a fine leather chair, a nice import, sipping his drink, also an import. Delicious, he thought, but what was more delicious was a good ol' victory to end your day with. And that he has gone oh so well. He relaxes, for the first time in a while. It's good to know everything has succeeded.
strings.BRA_lacerda.12.desc:
Lacerda's failed. He failed the election, and he failed the coup. Peaceful and violent transitions into power failed for him, and it was time to transition into a different country; hopefully, unlike all of his ambitions, and his attempts at power, and his plans, the helicopter will not fail.

It was a detailed plan, aimed to get Carlos Lacerda out of Brazil swiftly, safely, and secretly. The beginning step was to get a helicopter, which landed close to his house. The pilot was a close ally whom Lacerda knew he could trust. The helicopter was not his way out; it simply took him away, to a private airstrip, where a private plane was waiting for him. There, he took himself and his possessions onto the private plane, also piloted by a trusted ally. From the plane, he would fly directly to America, where he would be able to safely seek refuge from those who would want to strike back at him for his attempts at power-grabbing.

In the private plane, thousands of feet above the ground, already hundreds of miles away from his home, Carlos was fuming. Everything has gone to hell, he thought. Nothing has gone as I wanted, and I've done nothing but make everything worse. God damn it. God damn it all to hell! Curse Goulart, and curse the cowardly officers, and curse the Americans that wouldn't give him enough help. Curse it all. But what's done is done. There are regrets he cannot change, but he knew he had no choice to accept what happened, and move on.
strings.BRA_lacerda.13.desc:
Goulart was defeated. Not in the proper, legal way he was supposed to be defeated, through the ballot box, the civic institutions meant specifically for the peaceful, legal, agreed-upon ways to move from one leader to the next. No. He won the elections, but that was just a battle, and he has proceeded to go on and lose the war. Lacerda has won, and his coup has won him control of Brazil.

In an unmarked car, Jango makes his unceremonious retreat from the country that he called home. Crossing the border, he makes his way into Uruguay. He had allies there, he hoped, who would be able to support him, and keep him safe from those who had already done so much harm to him, his image, his home, his country. It was a defeat, and it was a retreat, and he just wanted to be done with it, done with it all.

Lacerda sits smugly at home, sipping his drink. He had won, after all this time and maneuvering, and he was happy to be done with the chaos of this political theater. God was victory sweet, almost as sweet as his drink.

“Mr. President!” said the assistant, coming into the room.

“God, what is it?”

“You are to be escorted to a safe room. Shots are being fired in Brasília.”
strings.BRA_lacerda.14.desc:
Carlos Lacerda, usurper of the Presidency of the United States of Brazil, was happy. Happy to have won the presidency not by the popular vote but by the will to pursue and achieve victory by any and all means necessary. Sadly for him, this seizure of power wouldn't come without consequences. The angry mobs chanting slogans in the streets gave the soon-to-be President flashbacks to the last time a bullet strayed him. It was decided as a precaution that his inauguration would be held in a bunker buried deep beneath Brasília.

With the bunker doors slowly swinging open, the President was welcomed by a cadre of army officials, police officers, American diplomats and a news crew, all quintessential to the plot that sent Goulart into exile and himself to the throne. With his left hand on the Bible and his right hand raised upward, Lacerda recited the oath of office, though now it was merely to give off the semblance of normalcy to an audience that knew better. By the time the oath was concluded, the President had turned to face the cameras to give his speech.

“People of Brazil, this is the day where true Brazilians triumph. In the face of Goulart's perversion of democracy, I had taken the initiative to beat back this communist insurrection and ensure our country didn't become a ”People's Republic“. Despite these unusual circumstances, I can assure you that the policies of the UDN have not changed in the slightest. I ask you, people of Brazil, to look to the bright future ahead of us, a future free from communist lies and Varguist tyranny, that together we can make Brazil greater than it has ever been. I thank you all for your unyielding support in these trying times and may God bless the United States of Brazil and its people.”

With his speech over, the Crow and his murder took flight from the bunker and into a now tense atmosphere.
strings.BRA_lacerda.14.a: The Crow clawed the tyrant and became one in his stead.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.1.desc:
Obscured by the tablecloth, the ambassador's wrinkled hands coiled and uncoiled the elaborate cloth napkin the Santiago embassy kept for these dinners.
