Chilean president-elect Raúl Rettig had taken only a single bite of his bobo de camarão. His second would-be spoonful lay there suspended over the steaming bowl of stew. Had his sources been wrong about the seafood? Had that blasted chef overheated the thing? The motionless spoon's half a prawn and dash of manioc provided no answer.

At least Rettig and Minister of Foreign Affairs Leitão da Cunha were talking. The two men who had more control over the ambassador's fate than any save President Carlos Lacerda himself had been sustaining a friendly, but formal dialogue for the past several minutes. Dialogue. Oh dear, he hadn't said a word. That blasted hypnotic prawn.

“Chile and Brazil are brought ever closer together by the machinations of Buenos Aires,” he chimed in, “From Bolivia to Antarctica, we jointly can and must resist their imperialist urges.” The ambassador took a bite of his own bobo to conceal his smile; he had emerged from his stasis with a single timely, prudent remark.

Rettig turned to the ambassador for the first time in the meal, spoon submerging the prawn into the manioc sea. “Our continent certainly has seen too many machinations lately.” Why did da Cunha blanch at that? Was this leftist making some veiled remark against-? “I'm looking forward to working with yourselves and President Lacerda.”

The ambassador saw Da Cunha glance at him, a bit of color returning to his face. The minister raised his glass, “A toast then. May we stand together...” he seemed to be restraining a laugh, “against imperialist urges.”

For the first time, Rettig's polite smile broke into a mirthful chuckle, and he raised his own glass.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.2.desc:
President Carlos Lacerda felt a small pang in his chest. The small antbird statuette was wordlessly being turned round and round in the deft hands of his Chilean counterpart, the newly-elected Julio Philippi Izquierdo. After what felt like a minute, Philippi set it down on the hardwood table with a satisfied “Delightful.”

Lacerda exhaled. Philippi had requested this visit to Brasília almost immediately following his election, sending the diplomatic service scrambling for an appropriate gift. Luckily, the Chilean technocrat's interest in ornithology was well known. “And thank you again for your gift” - framed Chilean newspaper articles covering Lacerda's election as governor of Guanabara “and for prioritizing a visit to the Palácio da Alvorada. Ours is going to be a fruitful partnership.”

Philippi nodded, “Your presidency is still young, but I confess to have been watching it with great interest. Overcoming its, em, inauspicious start, you have made the right moves to modernize public administration. Your forceful approach to countering Argentina's spreading influence is very welcome in Santiago. For the first, Chile will be confined to providing moral support, and perhaps learning from example. But on Buenos Aires, I look forward to working with you side-by-side.”

Lacerda was taken aback, and it was Philippi who rose first and offered a hand. But the Crow met his grip enthusiastically, “I wish you and Chile the finest of luck in the months ahead; I hope that they are filled with more visits to the Palácio.”

“And I wish the same to you, Carlos.” Philippi cracked a smile and offered a small wink, “If you keep providing me with birds such as these, I will have to!”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.2.a: If only all diplomacy was this easy.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.3.desc:
“How in the hell did the Chileans elect a literal Nazi?!” Carlos Lacerda bellowed.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Leitão da Cunha prayed that the door of the presidential office had withstood the outburst, or at least that the Palace's resident gossips were out for the day. “Jorge Prat thankfully left the National Socialist party, but I agree that his far right stances are worrying.”

“So he's an opportunistic bastard, content to be a Nazi whenever it's convenient. I'm so relieved, Vasco,” Lacerda's lips coiled into a sneer. “We're going to do three things. One, I want the Chilean embassy to go dark. No events, no dinners. We let Prat know that I loathe him just as much as he hates me. Two, we make the only exception. We talk to the fascist bastards, cooperate with them even, if and only if they want to move against Argentina. Prat will be gone in a few years, but the gaucho threat will remain.”

Leitão da Cunha scribbled down hurried notes - 'no contact' and 'anti-Argentina only' before meeting the President's eyes once more. “And the third, Your Excellency?”

“You get a copy of every issue of that Estanquero magazine Prat published. And you get whoever is staffing our embassy in Chile to use their newfound free time to report back every heinous piece of Nazi trash that crossed the bastard's broken mind. Be sure to capture the most idiotic points. We, and the Chileans, need to know what kind of filth their new leader is made of.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.4.desc:
As part of his new office, Lacerda received plenty of newspapers to read first thing in the morning. He preferred O Estado de S. Paulo, didn't mind Gazeta do Povo, found an illicit thrill in Notícias Populares, and ranged from distaste to disgust with the rest. But no matter what newspaper he read, they were all talking about the same thing.

SALVADOR ALLENDE WINS CHILE ELECTION! The first time he read this, it was as if he'd lost the power of literacy. He had to re-read the headline several times, cross-reference it with the front pages of other newspapers to be sure he was not hallucinating. He knew of Allende, knew the wily little socialist had been making moves in Chile, but this?

NEW GOVERNMENT'S COMMITMENT TO SOCIALISM AFFIRMED! Lacerda felt light-headed with panic. He'd only just started, and already he was dealing with a potential problem on his western front. Chile used to be so reliable, so guaranteed to be a partner. Now that support was less guaranteed. He could see the red over that vertical strip of land, like skin being flayed off to reveal muscle.

TENSIONS WITH BRAZIL RISE AFTER ALLENDE'S PREVIOUS COMMENTS! What comments? Lacerda searched back through his mind's archive, trying to remember if he dealt with him before. And then it came back to him: God, he called him a fascist, didn't he? In one of his fucking rags?

With a small roar, Lacerda threw the newspapers off his desk, knocking off a paperweight and a small collection of pens. It was a feeble discharge of energy, but it knocked him out of his loathing and helped center himself. He slumped back in his chair, mouth slightly agape. Chile was now no longer a reliable partner. They were now a problem. He dreaded the inevitable confrontation with Argentina, now that he was down one partner.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.4.a: God, he thought, if only things could have gone differently down there...
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.5.desc:
Bottles clinked as Lacerda sought the right poison for the occasion. Something bitter. Something strong. Something red. A Chilean pinot noir lurked on the bottom shelf. Apt.

He uncorked it and took a long, hefty swig. Allende. Of all the disgraces Chile could have chosen it picked the socialist. Soon-to-be communist. The man who would turn the mountainous republic into a dictatorship and its idiotic voters into slaves.

The burning rush of wine down his throat made the president cough and splutter, coating the presidential desk with red droplets. The official cable notifying him of Allende's victory, of Brazil and the OFN's total defeat, was splattered and stained. A dark laugh erupted from somewhere inside Lacerda... they'd have to file this document away somewhere. A memorial to disgrace.

Another gulp of wine, more measured this time. What did this mean for Brazilian foreign policy? Abandoned to fight Argentina alone, alienated from an ailing ally? Ally no more - Chilean communists would be propping up their ideological spawn throughout Latin America. A second front opening up for Brazil...

Lacerda, unwilling to relinquish his bottle, fumbled with the phone in his off-hand. Only one ring, and one swig, later, Minister of Foreign Affairs Leitão da Cunha picked up. And Lacerda said,
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.5.a: “Tell the Santiago embassy to pack up. We're breaking off relations with Chile.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.6.desc:
...It is at this moment that I call upon the Chilean people, whose legacy of soldiery upholds their national mythos as the scabbard on the saber belt of South America, to do everything in their power to undermine the radical regime in Santiago! It is Allende and his dalliance with extremism that threatens to uproot the prosperity that we have all worked so hard to achieve in favor of a red dictatorship! Let Brazil's example be a warning to all; Radicalism in Chile shall find no ally in Brasília or anywhere in the Southern Cone where national sovereignty still reigns paramount!“

He did not take that well. As of earlier that week, the Brazilian ambassador to Chile thought dully, or rather, the former ambassador. The flight from Santiago to Brasília was a middle class charter flight. It would take some time, enough for the newspaper to function as a distraction when the admittedly pretty sight of the Amazon out of the window grew repetitive. Opting out of flying first class felt like a prudent gesture; better to ingratiate oneself to the common man in light of the recent election than not.

Of course, he had already heard Lacerda's speech on the radio when he was packing his bags to return to Brazil, who hadn't? The velvet rope revolution Santiago had at the ballot box would only anger everyone close to Chile, none more so than Lacerda. He assumed the closing of the Brazilian Embassy was coming well before it was announced, and truthfully, he felt little concern over it all. There was plenty of work to be found back in the home capital, and even if Lacerda wanted to throw a foreign policy hissy fit over Allende, it would never amount to much of anything.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.6.a: He produced a BIC lighter and a cigar from his pockets as he leaned back in his seat.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.7.desc:
The mood was jubilant at the Moneda. When Lacerda had heard of Frei's victory in the Chilean elections, the Brazilian president wasted no time in drafting up the plans to send Foreign Minister Leitão da Cunha to congratulate the new Chilean President and ensure the beginnings of a strong partnership. Frei was, by all accounts, an improvement over the old Alessandri regime - and would certainly be willing to partner with Brazil and the OFN more broadly. If he played his cards right, Lacerda could turn Chile's success into something even more fruitful.

Frei had been nothing but a courteous and statesmanly host, warmly welcoming the foreign ministers and heads of state who attended his inaugural celebration. Leitão had wanted to get some time to speak with the new president in a greater capacity past a handshake and a sentence or two of platitudes, and so he had to wait past the celebratory speeches and the chicken dinner to catch more than a brief moment.

“Foreign Minister, I am glad to see you. How are you finding the evening's festivities?” Frei was all smiles as he shook Leitão's hand.

“I find them quite well, Mister President. President Lacerda congratulates you on your victory and wishes to convey to you that you have a willing friend and partner in his Presidency. He hopes that we can work together to bring peace and prosperity to the continent.”

“That is appreciated.” Frei's smile kept wide, but the corners of his eyes sharpened. “I respect President Lacerda's foreign relations with the US and his preservation of Brazilian democracy, I have some...misgivings of him as a person.”

Leitão paused for a moment as he absorbed Frei's diplomatic way of saying that he hated Lacerda's guts. “Well, even despite all that, he and I both believe we can work with you. Allow me to toast your success.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.7.a: The President chuckled, nodded with understanding, and accepted the toast with a clink.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.8.desc:
Once again, Lacerda held his pen in his hand, pondering the message he had written as a memo in front of him. “Mr. Santander, you have my deepest condolences for the death of your predecessor. To lose a magnificent and beloved leader before his time is a tragedy, and my heart is with those mourning his loss.” He had written, then rewritten it several times. It was only a procedural message, sure, but going too far risked being interpreted as reconciliatory by its emissaries.

A knock. One of his secretaries was bringing in new files, halting only to ask about his upcoming schedule, and for his responses to those previously brought in. Lacerda still had more than enough time, but he still decided to give the memo over, ordering it to be transferred, first to the Brazilian embassy in Buenos Aires, and then directly to the Argentinian government. Only one more paper to add to the pile of his counterpart's desk, but he was hopeful that it wouldn't be forgotten.

Lacerda stopped himself once again, now deep in thought. Rarely had an Argentinian politician attracted his attention, let alone approval, nearly as much as Silvano Santander had. Few men had been as staunch an opponent of authoritarianism as Santander had been. Even fewer still had been such an open critic of Juan Perón, and had been arrested in the defence of freedom. Truly, Santander could have been a valuable ally against fascism, against communism, and against Nazism.

If only. Lacerda was many things, but a fantasist was not one. Peronism had not quite broken out of Argentina, but he knew the Varguists weren't far behind. They would do everything in their power, he thought, to defend a contagious strain of their worldview. The military, too, had a lot to gain from their current antagonism with Argentina, and would not stand for any form of rapprochement. Perhaps, in another world, their administrations could have ushered in an age of regional peace and liberty.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.8.a: And so, with time to burn, Lacerda spent it on things that could never be.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.9.desc:
Firmly grasping the paper in his hands, Carlos Lacerda read over its report one last time. After an intensely-fought election, the Radical Civic Union, headed by Rodolfo Martinovic had won. Lacerda knew better than to ever publicly intercede - to do so would be shrugged off as an unfunny joke by his ideological opponents, and would be electoral suicide for his ideological allies - but he also knew better than to simply write this off as irrelevant to his future policy.

It did not take knowing about the minutiae of Argentine politics to know what Martinovic's victory represented. The left-wing nationalism advanced by Hipólito Yrigoyen, and the antagonism it provided towards the United States, boded poorly for him. Its arguments and views, ultimately, were not truly far from those of the Varguism he'd spent decades of his life working against. Once again, he sighed, setting down the newspaper. Another country had embraced ideological insanity.

But, Lacerda thought, worse candidates could still have won. The UCRP, for all of its flaws, still ultimately supported the democratic process. What speeches he had heard from Martinovic at least came with an intense revulsion from fascism, and the reports he had received on internal dynamics indicated that this was not a fringe stance of his among UCRP adherents. If nothing else, they weren't outright Peronists, and the supporters of that ousted tyrant were licking their wounds.

Perhaps this was not the worst case scenario. The Radicals would attain power, they would struggle with implementing rational policy, the voters would find themselves increasingly alienated, and provided that the Peronists didn't worm themselves back into the minds of the electorate, they would turn back to sanity and vote for a more right-leaning government that would come to power with minimal fuss. Even still, he thought, best not to give them the acknowledgement that others deserve.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.9.a: The best and worst of no worlds.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.10.desc:
Holding the paper in one hand, Carlos Lacerda read over its report one last time. He knew better than to ever intervene in Argentine politics - but he also knew better than to simply ignore everything that happened there. A victory for an aligned faction could really help him. And, as his eyes lifted off the pages, he knew that it had. Emilio Jofré, and the National Federation of Centrist Parties, had managed to win, pushing a tightly-contested election down to the wire.

However, it was not Jofré himself that Lacerda's interest was drawn to. The man himself, whilst agreeable, was only one of a hundred factors. It was the wider Argentine conservative movement that drew his gaze, and the implications of their victory. He had once stopped watching over their rise, but Lacerda now cursed himself for not being more attentive. These were reasonable men, and if not removed immediately, would become valuable, southern partners to him.

With that, Lacerda placed down the report, leaning backwards into his seat. Even calling them reasonable men was a disservice to them. These were devoted anti-fascists, ones open to negotiation and common sense, rejecting the far-left and far-right in equal measure. It would be difficult to go over the military's plans for the region, perhaps, but establishing firm relations between himself and this new government as a means of combatting extremism was a worthy end by itself.

Almost reflexively, Carlos Lacerda turned to his desk, bringing a piece of paper to his typewriter to offer his congratulations. He was sure that it'd only be considered for a second by Jofré's incoming government, but it was a valuable start, one that could percolate across the movement and breathe sanity into the region once again. New trade deals, reduced military presence, and a strengthened commitment to international justice could all serve as planks in cooling mutual frustrations.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.10.a: If only he could go all the way and end this Cold War.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.11.desc:
Firmly grasping the paper in his hands, Carlos Lacerda read over its report one last time, the paper folded down by the pressure of gravity, and under his hawkish gaze. After a tight contest, Guillermo Estévez Boero and the Popular Socialist Party had managed to push themselves into power. Even with the limited attention he had devoted to Argentinian politics, the prospect of an Boero presidency still filled Lacerda with a degree of real sorrow.

He knew all too well what Boero represented, and just how far it diverged from his idea of sanity. Total codification, and the unification within Argentina, the coalescence of nationalism and leftism into a toxic ideology, coalesced by turning away from Berlin to designate the United States as the beating heart of fascism, and all of its allies as collaborators. Lacerda's stomach turned at the prospect, one that he viewed as unforgivable, and one that he knew would not invite any means of softening the Cold War.

Lacerda also knew all too well where Boero had come from. A student activist, Boero had spent much of the last decade riling up students, misplacing their woes and directing their anger into his personal enrichment. They had done that well, Lacerda thought, shaking his head. How he had gone beyond that base of unkempt, unrefined radicals to allow the Argentine populace to feverishly enable his rise to power was an issue that Lacerda struggled to justify. Even Goulart, he thought, wasn't as radical.

Bringing out another sheet of paper, Carlos Lacerda began to write. He knew better, even now, than to completely break what relations Brazil still shared. The powder keg was even closer to firing than normal, and there were better strategies Brasília could employ than justifying revanchism on both ends of the border. Instead, Lacerda decided to probe potential avenues that Brazil could use to benefit from the situation, so long as he viewed Boero as merely troubling.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.11.a: Dancing on the edge of oblivion.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.12.desc:
Carlos Lacerda always liked to consider himself a refined man, one firmly aligned with the causes of justice and liberty. Vargas' regime had ensured that he would never feel any sympathy towards him, or his successors. He knew better than to believe that the socialism of João Goulart or Kubitschek was fundamentally different from those thugs that had previously tried to kill him, or to ever let up on them. To lift his gaze from them for even an instant would be time aplenty for them to pounce.

And so, he felt a burning rage as he heard of the results from Argentina. They could disguise themselves in a million different ways, and they could attempt to embrace a billion different disguises, but the cracks in their ideology always showed. No matter how much they claimed to cling to ideals of “Justicialism”, he would not be tricked into ever viewing them as anything other than a ghost, a Trojan Horse through which Peronism could return across the Río de la Plata.

It didn't take much to lift their veil. Their foreign policy was exactly as antagonistic as any diplomat could fear, their economic policy was as ludicrous as Perón's own, their embrace of fascism as whole-hearted and repulsive, their national enemies were drawn in the same visage. Every aspect remained from top to bottom, only loosely hidden beneath the disguise of a smile. Lacerda didn't know whether to hold them more in contempt or the fools tricked into supporting this reheated nonsense.

But if he wanted to move, he had to act fast, and smart. He found their government repulsive, sure, but breaking off relations with Argentina entirely would not only jeopardise any thinking Argentine still left, but would throw Brazil dangerously close to the edge. But he wouldn't just accept this new order as a natural, irreversible state. The moment those supposed Peronists without Perón were to allow their military to show their true colours, he would be more than ready.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.12.a: The numbers for diplomats representing neighbouring powers echoed in his head once more.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.13.desc:
The newspaper crumpled beneath Lacerda's white-knuckled grip, the face of president-to-be Juan Perón's face distorting. A drop of sweat landed on the headline of “PERON TO RETURN FROM EXILE.” With a roar of rage, Lacerda split the photo in half. “Fucking fascists! Entire nation of people who think of nothing but violence!” He spat.

Of course, he prayed for God's wrath to strike down Perón's plane before he touched down in Buenos Aires. If God wasn't merciful enough, he had to act before the bastard took power. From here on out, he wouldn't have a second to breathe. Nowhere in South America would be safe from Argentine influence, and every resource will have to be spent to keep Brazil and her neighbors safe.

He couldn't wait for Perón to strike the first blow. Brazil would have to commit more to the military. More soldiers. More tanks. More fighters. More missiles. Any kind of relationship with Argentina would have to be broken. It would only be helping. As Perón flew over the Atlantic, Brazil's embassy staff was coming home.

Lacerda stared at the bisected face of the devil himself. He was ready for his games, whatever they may be. All there was left to do was to say another prayer for victory.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.14.desc:
The news of Arambaru's ascension to the Argentinean Presidency was a warm relief to Carlos Lacerda, as if it marked an end to all the madness that preceded it, the carousel of strongmen putting on their best caudillo impressions.

It was a welcome breath of fresh air, not just for him, but for all of South America. With reasonable men managing the two largest democracies on the continent, there was a real chance for peace by putting an end to their Cold War, by returning their lands to normality. Even if Arambaru's democracy seemed more like window-dressing at times, his intentions were noble, and that was what really mattered.

With that, he made a note, to be transferred to the relevant ministries. The government line on Argentina would change to one of critical support, spread through state institutions and sympathetic media outlets. Through this, closer ties with the new regime could be formed, and a happier continent for all.

At least, that was how Lacerda ideally pictured it. In practice, it would be far harder, but a man was allowed to dream.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.14.a: A managed response to a managed democracy.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.15.desc:
Their Brazilian embassy in Chile had sent the letter a week ago. Now, Adhemar turned over a copy of that exact same letter in his hands. It was perfect: a neat, soulless congratulation to President Rettig following his victory in the elections — and not a single orthographic error!

The only thing Adhemar wanted in return was a similarly soulless tip of the hat from the Chileans. Was that too much to ask for? But no. Nothing. No reply. No phone call. Not a single nod from across the Andes.

And Adhemar wasn't having it. “Keep things polite,” he ordered the embassy staff during a meeting. “Polite, but distant. If they want to talk, they can come with their own letters.”

The diplomats understood. No outreach. No initiatives. No favors. If Rettig wanted to play coy, so be it — but he'd be playing alone. Brazil wasn't about to drop to its knees and beg for attention.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.15.a: It's not like Adhemar could do anything about it.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.16.desc:
On the third floor of the Planalto Palace, President Adhemar de Barros gave his golden pen another lazy twirl. The briefing on newly elected Chilean president Julio Philippi Izquierdo had grown several pages from its previous incarnation, back when Philippi had been a mere candidate. Notes on his campaign promises, modest to Adhemar's taste. Notes on his work in Alessandri's cabinet, all dutiful enough. A footnote on Phillipi's studies so large that it alone might reach to Santiago. But nothing with which to hook this ideological void into tighter ties with Brazil.

Adhemar stilled the pen mid-sweep. He had it. The nib plunged to a sheet of loose paper on his desk, scratching out a promise of prosperity. Or at least the first draft of one. Always pleasant to practice his Spanish.

Your Excellency,

The people of Brazil, and myself foremost among them, count ourselves lucky to see the Chilean presidency in such sure hands. The leadership and acumen you displayed in your former role in the Ministry of Economy will now surely lift Chile up to new heights of wealth, creating opportunities for commerce and trade as welcome in São Paulo as they are in Valparaíso. Know that I personally and Brazilian business as a collective, wish to see you succeed in your ambitions, and are eager to begin discussing how we can strengthen economic relations between our two states. You are welcome, as my guest, in Brasília at any time. I promise you a most enriching experience.

And with one last twist of the pen, he signed,
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.17.desc:
Your Excellency,

I read with great anticipation the victor of Chile's elections, and was very pleased to see the name Jorge Prat atop my briefing this morning. My warmest congratulations.

While we haven't yet grown personally acquainted, everything that I read about you suggests that Santiago and Brasília will grow closer than ever during our presidencies. Your faith guides you as mine does me, and I hear you also have a healthy respect for the economic benefits of private initiative. Your forthright statements on the perils of Argentine aggression suggest that our foreign policies will align.

Some of your speeches on the campaign trail heralded understandable skepticism to the overweening role played by North Americans in the Chilean economy. I assure you that Brazil - its businesses, its financiers, and its president, stand ready to assist your nation as it looks to diversify its markets and sources of investment. May our partnership be a renewed font of prosperity on both sides of the Andes.

Yours faithfully,
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.18.desc:
President Adhemar de Barros had today's paper stretched taut between his hands. But next month's, next year's headlines were plain to see: 'Chilean Capital Flight Intensifies', 'Santiago Announces Further Nationalizations', 'LATAM Socialists Convene in Valparaíso'. All bound up in those five little words: 'Shock Victory for Allende in Chile'.

Adhemar tore the paper in two. 'Shock' - 'Allende in Chile' now lay across his desk. What did they pay those intelligence analysts for? They'd assured him that it would be the moralizer Frei at worst. Instead Brazil's Pacific partner was barrelling down this Chilean road to socialism, with a quick pitstop at national and international crisis.

A twitch of the mouth and Adhemar swept the papers into the wastebasket by his side. He reached for the phone. Who to call first? 'Shock'. Ministry of Foreign Affairs - how bold would Argentina become now? 'Allende'. PSP party headquarters - what was this doing for his ratings? Allende 'in Chile' had been calling him a robber baron on the campaign trail for weeks... So many numbers in his head - 'Shock'- that Adhemar's fingers followed on their most practiced course.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.18.a: “This is de Barros. Liquidate all my Chilean holdings.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.19.desc:
“Frei, huh,” said President Adhemar de Barros, voice flat as he leafed through the morning's briefing.

“Certainly not the worst president Chile could have elected,” replied Foreign Minister Leitão da Cunha, taking his place at the Palácio's long table. “Personally, I am hopeful that President Frei will be able to address Chile's long-running rural challenges. Head off instability and socialism and give us a firmer partner against Argentina.”

“I'm hopeful that our relations will remain cold rather than strained. All his grand, pie-in-the-sky plans on education, in the fields, across the globe, and with their copper remind me of Kubitschek. Could be who Frei wanted to see in the Planalto - it certainly wasn't me.” The President set the briefing aside and beckoned an aide for drafting paper.

As Adhemar's gold pen glided back and forth across the page, Leitão da Cunha ventured yet again, “I would be happy to work with our Chilean experts at the Ministry to draft a congratulatory letter for your signature. Could free some time ahead of your meeting with Natel.”

Adhemar lifted and then shook his head with a toothy grin and a trace of his usual charm, “No, no. Nothing more vital than that personal connection.” His gaze returned to the page, “And where else do I get to show my mastery of formal, cordial, and outright dull Spanish?” The two shared a brief chuckle, before the President said,
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.19.a: “Wouldn't have minded a different audience though.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.20.desc:
“Palacios is dead. This new Argentine, Silvano Santander, is putting up a valiant fight against rigor mortis to see if he can be more rigid and inflexible than his predecessor,” spat President Adhemar de Barros. Foreign Minister Leitão da Cunha struggled to hide a grimace at the crude remark, but de Barros continued his rant without noticing.“Santander - this man is a cosseted elite who has never spoken with ordinary folks, let alone done anything for them. And he never will! Santander will do nothing for the welfare of his people, because he has no taste for the feel, the grit, the realities of politics. A little oligarchic saint sitting there on his pillar condemning the world!”

The President was pacing back and forth across his Planalto office now, rays of sunlight breaking and reappearing as he past, “Santander whines about communists, he jumps at imaginary Nazis. Thinks the fascists are trying to bring down his government. He will do that himself, no need for any fascists!”

Leitão da Cunha tried to stand stock still, to follow the outraged President with only his eyes. “And that is why, Vasco, this annoying mosquito of a man will accuse me, accuse this administration of being fascist. To deflect from his own failings. And when Santander makes that move, Brazil must be ready.”

Leitão da Cunha's mouth moved before his head could halt it, “To do what, Mr. President?”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.20.a: “To fight. If Argentina wants a fight, they'll get it.”
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.21.desc:
Adhemar had just finished writing his latest letter: a message of congratulations to the new Radical government in Argentina. President Rodolfo Martinovic had earned his victory rightfully, establishing himself as a new paragon for Argentinean democracy, giving new life to the prospects of peace between Argentina and Brazil so that they may blah blah blah...

In truth, Adhmemar considered Martinovic to be weird, not unusual in Argentine politics, but he was noticeably odd. He seemed to endlessly blather on about anti-imperialism, about America being the great evil of this world, a lot like that poor soul Quadros. His more left-wing tendencies left something to be desired too.

However, Adhemar could keenly recognize a fellow populist when he saw one. With that, there was opportunity, if both parties could spin it that way. For instance, a business deal can always be portrayed as the creation of new jobs to enrich workers and families, rather than a narrative of capitalist exploitation droned on by communists and misanthropes.

So, Adhemar was content, content that Martinovic would see things his way. If not, maybe a little gift would act as an extra incentive, an envelope of a different kind.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.21.a: With two populists, they should be twice as popular!
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.22.t: On Behalf of the Brazilian People
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.22.desc:
Adhemar tapped the stillborn letter with his pen. “On behalf of the Brazilian people,” what? As president, it should be his job to speak for his nation — hell, that's why the people voted for him! But co-signing the letter directed at the Argentinian Conservatives felt wrong. The Brazilian people didn't want this. He wanted this.

Say what you want about them (and Adhemar certainly did have much to say), but they did want détente. They were elitist bastards who wanted to lock the world in amber, but they did want détente. They barely cared for the common people, but they did want détente. Adhemar didn't understand how they'd returned to Argentina, but they did want-

By now, his pen had left a dark inkblot. Without much fanfare, Adhemar threw draft #3 into the pile and reached for another empty sheet of paper. Were there any redeeming qualities in the new Argentinian government? If nothing else, Adhemar was rather fond of that Jofré individual. He was a conservative — yes — but something told him that man was more lucid than his decomposing peers (especially when it came to the economy).

“To the Government of the Argentine Republic,
On behalf of the Brazilian administration and its people, I extend our heartfelt congratulations on the inauguration of President Emilio Jofré. May this mark the beginning of a renewed chapter of friendship and cooperation between our two nations and across South America.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.22.a: This time, with a little more heart.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.23.desc:
The newspaper shook in Adhemar's hands as he read the news: Guillermo Estévez Boero had won the Argentinean elections. He had only gotten halfway through the first page of the story before he had dropped the papers entirely and began to laugh. A deep laugh, straight from the heart.

It was ridiculous. The world had to be playing some kind of poor joke on him for a student activist to become the leader of Brazil's rival nation during Adhemar's tenure as President. For as long as Adhemar could remember, his career had been dotted with student activists protesting perfectly ordinary politicking and policies, barking like dogs over tiny details like a politician getting some benefits from his own hard work, or a pragmatic choice in who won a contract.

Adhemar picked the newspaper off of the floor and set it aside. If this is the hand fate dealt him, at least it was an interesting one. Adhemar would have to keep an eye on the situation, but he relished the anticipation of what was to come as he picked up his pen.

After all, Boero, despite everything, seemed like a man that could be negotiated with, and so there wasn't any reason to burn bridges yet. A simple congratulations letter was all that was needed to get the ball rolling.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.23.a: When it comes to the fates of nations, everyone learns to compromise.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.24.desc:
“Peronists Win Argentinean Elections” read the headlines in great bold font, displaying the news to anyone who picked up a newspaper. Adhemar had always thought that Perón had some great ideas, and he was more than happy to see that the people of Argentina had finally agreed.

Adhemar had wanted to make some new friends in Argentina, and this new Cipriano Reyes fellow and his government presented the perfect opportunity. Adhemar quickly swapped out the newspaper in his hands for a pen, as he began writing a letter of congratulations.

Many congratulations, much praise, and one promise to personally attend the inauguration of Reyes later, Adhemar put the pen down, satisfied. It had only taken a single draft, and it felt like the fastest official letter he had ever written as President. Adhemar was sure this was going to be the beginnings of a wonderful relationship between Brazil and Argentina, and hoped that both their governments could work together to bring prosperity and an end to the brother wars in South America. He'd personally make sure the letter got mailed out as quickly as possible.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.24.a: Peace surely lies ahead for both our nations.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.25.desc:
Alberto Campos sat still in his office. Around him was a ticking clock, the soft rustling of the wind outside, the restless tapping of his foot; these were all distractions from the sound he dreaded and desired to hear. He could feel his breath cycling through his lungs, with its slow, unsteady pace. When the phone finally rang, Campos lunged at it.

“Mr. Campos, is that you?” From the other end of the line, he heard smacking lips. “This is Adhemar de Barros. How do you do?”

Campos' blood chilled. “Good evening, Mr. President. I'm fine. How are you?”

“Splendid, Alberto. Do you mind if I call you Alberto?” A pause, no more than a second; Alberto's body and tongue were painfully still. “Well, Alberto, I have a number of friends with planes that we can charter. They'll get your man from Madrid to Buenos Aires without any suspicions being raised.” The voice on the other end of the line was cool, lacking the flop sweat on Campos' forehead. “I'd love to give him something more fitting, but one has to be discreet with these things.”

Campos clutched the telephone and braced his elbow on the desk to keep his hand from shaking. “Argentina thanks you. We won't soon forget this.”

“Of course, of course. Say hello to Perón for me when he arrives. Good night, Mr. Campos.”

Adhemar de Barros placed the receiver back in his cradle, and his smile fell with it. He wiped away sweat from his brow, rose and made his way to his liquor cabinet. He grabbed the first bottle he saw, along with a glass and some ice. As he poured the liquid whose label he'd not checked into the glass, he caught his uncertain face in the mirror. He took the glass and raised it...
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.25.a: ...a silent toast to the man he prayed was best for Brazil and Argentina.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.26.t: A Northern Thaw or a Southern Slow Burn?
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.26.desc:
Adhemar de Barros' limousine hustled along the boulevard with practiced pugnaciousness, the statesman's visage looking onto the passing frescas of Brasília like a cartoon, the rotating canvas of old European architecture stitched onto the Amazon as a backdrop; The meeting with Argentine ambassador had gone better than it ought to have, de Barros quietly musing on the implications of it behind crossed legs and steepled fingers. Is this a foundation that can be built upon? de Barros pondered.

Aramburu's election victory was a welcome diversion from the typically gloomy news coming out of Buenos Aires, the moderate progressive platform doing much to sap support from the left and the right in Argentina. Politics had the potential to become predictable in the Southern Cone, easily manageable and even beneficial to Brazil for a change, assuming his less savory tendencies could be kept in check.

That having been said, de Barros' experience as a Paulista politico meant that Aramburu's brand of otherwise benign egalitarianism was going to work on him; Adhemar could tell right away what kind of manipulative bastard the new Argentine president was, as he himself had made his bones reducing these kinds of backroom desk mice into stepping stones for more proven leadership.

Aramburu's real issues revolved around his foreign policy, something that hardly dovetailed with the interests of their northern neighbor.; The OFN commitments were perhaps predictable after a generation or more of trying to walk backwards from Perón's excesses, but it made de Barros' job more difficult in trying to secure Brazilian neutrality. Maybe Buenos Aires' leadership could be negotiated into something more mutually accommodating with Brasília, but, until then, maintaining a vigilant eye and a guarded approach to Argentina's new leadership seemed to be the order of the day.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.27.desc:
The news of the UCRP's victory in the Argentine elections brought a smile to Edna's face, a respite in a hectic time. She didn't follow their politics too avidly, but the Radicals were singing from the same Hymn sheet as the PTB, even if they were singing to different choirs.

These differences were made acutely aware to her as she read about Martinovic's speech. “Peace will never be an option as long as America has a presence in our continent.” “We only know one imperialism here, and its capital is not Tokyo, but Washington.” “Argentina will not bow to foreign tyranny.” It was all exhausting, but she figured it was what his audience wanted.

She also figured that Martinovic was a politician, and like all the politicians she had become familiar with thanks to Adhemar, his words would be a lot softer if he wasn't put on a pedestal. So, Edna made the first move, writing out a florid letter of congratulations. It would be a work of art, something that would soften him up for when she met him at the inauguration.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.27.a: Is there nothing better than left-wing cooperation?
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.28.desc:
The Conservative Party in Argentina was something Edna regarded as a museum piece, an assortment of old men who thought life was better when women didn't have the vote, or when only they could vote. Her reaction that they had claimed victory in their most recent election was suitably disappointed upon hearing the news, feeling a bit of sick come up out of her throat.

When she studied the news further, her reaction tempered somewhat. Their new President, Emilio Jofré, was somewhat distinct from the usual Conservative stereotypes. After listening to a brief biography presented to her by an assistant, she felt more relaxed knowing he wasn't an oligarchical ogre, but someone from the twentieth century able to stomach women being in politics.

More pressingly, the Conservative Party — despite lingering regressive attitudes — were doves when it came to the South American Cold War, notably advocating for detente between Argentina and Brazil. It was almost as if their election was her wish regarding a moremore peaceful and prosperous Latin America answered.

And so, she happily began writing down a letter of congratulations, with a realigned attitude to her new neighbor ruling party.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.28.a: A sigh of relief for peace.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.29.desc:
When Edna first heard that the Socialist Party had triumphed, there was a smile on her face. As the news trickled in, the smile became subdued, albeit still there.

Newly-elected Guillermo Estévez Boero could not help himself but play-up the typical anti-American sentiments, acting as if they were in anyway comparable to the fascist rulers of Europe, alongside some symptoms of the traditional nationalist chest-beating all too common to Argentina.

However, there was potential. Boero was a former student activist, a group she knew very well from her time teaching, and a group she could easily talk to. With their shared left-wing ideals, there was certainly potential to shape the new President, turn him to her side. No reason why both their nationalisms couldn't peacefully co-exist.

His impending inauguration would prove to be an ideal opportunity for this, so she made sure to prep him with her letter of congratulations.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.29.a: Where one sees challenge, others see potential.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.30.desc:
The sound of Edna Lott tapping her fingernails would have driven any guest in her office mad, fortunately for her, she kept her flagrant irritation more or less private. She had spent most of the afternoon on the telephone, with everyone from foreign dignitaries to her colleagues in cities along the Argentine border to opposition leadership, all to a wide variety of decibels reflecting the dour mood in the Altiplano.

Perón. Edna thought contemptuously. Perón again. Not even a generation removed, and the acolytes of Argentina's most corrosive Admiral dictator had returned to Buenos Aires. Cipriano Reyes might be a fresher face compared to his predecessor. Still, the impetus had hardly changed: Presidential Imperialism and Pestilential Nationalism, however, couched in the language of progressive half-measures to keep widespread antipathy at a minimum.

As much as Edna could feel the painful period Argentina was about to enter into, her job remained more or less the same. Brazil could not just slam the door on Buenos Aires just yet, and there was enough window for Reyes to prove himself more amicable than Perón. Negotiations, trade deals, and maybe even military co-assistance. Nothing was off the table so long as the Justicialists could play nice.

Not all was lost for Brazil's southern neighbor either, as the more moderate progressive stances on labour and women's rights was a tendency that the forward-thinking people of Argentina could extrapolate. Perón himself, vile as he was, supported Vargas' return to Brazil decades before, a decision that allowed for a freer political environment for Brazil in the long run; What would her political career have been had that not happened? It was a venal suggestion, but maybe the same logic could be applied if Reyes truly was on the level?

If nothing else, it couldn't hurt to try.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.31.desc:
“Mr. President?”

Pedro Aleixo took a moment to look up at his aide. He still struggled with the title; he didn't expect to keep it, so he kept it only at arm's length. “Yes?”

“Mr. President, there's some news you should know about.” The aide handed over a telegram from the consulate in Buenos Aires.

“Oh,” he said, picking up the telegram. “{arg_getleader}. Have Foreign Affairs write up a statement. 'Congratulations, good luck'; keep it boilerplate.”

The aide took a moment before nodding, taking back the telegram and walking off to arrange the communiqué. As the door to his office closed, Aleixo kept staring at the wall. Argentina had a new president, and he struggled to care. He had plenty of problems just managing Brazil through this chaos; he didn't want to think about a country that, at least from his position, seemed to be doing better. That would be left to his successor, who would be chosen by the Brazilian people, who could bear the consequences of holding the title close to them.

He thought it prudent not to meddle in things that did not concern him, and right now his concern was making sure that the PSP emerged from Adhemar's death as strong as possible. He thought this was a matter best left to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. So he didn't bother thinking about it after this.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.32.desc:
Távora watched the television with a muted curiosity, watching the speech of the new Argentinian president, the cheering crowds and fluttering flags surrounding him. The afternoon had felt otherwise banal, the characteristic heat in Brasília persistent even in Távora's well air-conditioned residence. He'd already seen the speech on the television at the Altoplano, but felt compelled to watch it again while he mulled over the issue of Argentina's new leadership at home.

Martinovic was certainly something different for the leadership in Buenos Aires, doubtless lingering damage from Perón's time in office helped propel the liberal radicals to presidential office. His bluntly Anti-American foreign policy proposals and the UCRP's prominent left-wing nationalist bent was far too close to Vargas and his successor cliques for Távora's liking, leaving a foul taste in his mouth.

That said, UCRP was certainly more committed to rehabilitating Argentine democracy than a couple of the past presidents combined. In addition, this made their politics easier to predict - liberals, even radical liberals, were a type, after all - which was invaluable for planning out regional diplomacy in advance. Távora was prudent first and foremost, meaning if there was common ground to be found with Martinovic and his platform, there was certainly room to ensure at least cordial relations between Brasília and Buenos Aires.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.32.a: Cool winds can chill hot water, which is as good as the Southern Cone can ask for in the shadow of the New Order.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.33.desc:
Restaurante Corcovado wasn't quite so busy that day, save for the distant rattle of paparazzi cameras in the distance as Távora had a pleasant afternoon meal. In the distance, the towering backside of Cristo Redentor loomed over him, the beaming summer sun cracking through the clouds to light up great stone edifice and cast a shadow over Rio de Janeiro as it had for generations.

Távora felt compelled to find otherworldly inspiration in penning his letter to Argentina's newly elected president, praying the lord might bless him with the right words to congratulate the leadership in Buenos Aires.; First impressions were important, after all. Távora hoped to perhaps attend Jofré's inauguration in a couple month's time, thinking it would be a good show of support for the Brazilian president to attend.

In truth, the recent election was more of a victory for Brazil than it was even for the Argentine conservatives. Finally, Brasília and Buenos Aires sported party leadership that shared ideals, but presidential leadership that was somewhat comparable. Távora and Jofré were very much alike in this regard, as pragmatists, as conservatives and as patriots.

So much of the history in the Southern Cone was defined by mutual animosity between the north and south. Now with a mutual mandate of prosperity and national sovereignty ensconced in both nations, that most coveted and most elusive state of affairs., Detente, was finally within reach for both their people after so many generations had suffered so immensely.

With a flourish, a grin and a cup of coffee at his lips, Távora signed the letter with his signature and resumed his lunch.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.33.a: At long last, a chance to make amends.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.34.desc:
Távora paced back and forth in front of the television with muted contempt, the air in the Altoplano thick with trepidation. He had been watching the recording of Guillermo Estévez Boero's rally in Buenos Aires over and over again, torn halfway between disbelief and mounting anxiety; After decades of anti-socialist repression, the heirs to that ancient fossil Alfredo Palacios had managed to hoodwink the Argentinians at the ballot box without even having to fire a shot.

The principal nation in the Southern Cone becoming a hotbed of socialist agitation, so soon after Guevara's gambit in Uruguay, was frightening enough on the face of it. Adding to this the PS and their unique blend of left-wing nationalism and particularly Anti-American slant to their foreign policy, it did not take a versed political analyst to see the already tumultuous relationships between Argentina and their neighbors become even more strained.

Távora at the very least had the foresight to keep Brazil's priorities in perspective, something that might be lost with less qualified and more inflexible leadership at the helm; In his mind's eye, he could see and hear the absolute conniption Carlos Lacerda was likely having at this moment. How Távora's successors would handle Boero was more elusive to him, as the unruly nature of the new socialism regime in the south made them unpredictable. Távora would simply have to hope and pray the men of his party would be up to the task.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.34.a: Távora continued to pace in front of the television.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.35.desc:
He had been on the phone with men of his party for what felt like the whole day and it was only mid-afternoon; Távora's head felt sweat beating down his brow as she shuffled around documents around his desk in every direction, phoning one colleague and another after another to compile a consensus on foreign policy to the sudden paradigm shift that just struck buenos Aires.

There comes a point in the life of even the most hard-bitten political operative that one has to draw the line somewhere; Távora was not naive, not anymore than Adhemar was. The Progressistas might have aspirations implied in their name, but they were definitively of the cynical type even to the layman. They knew what they were, said what they wanted loud and clear, and were perfectly willing to tilt in the name of their platform...but there was such a thing as too far, even to the students of de Barros.

Even they struggled to find a more fitting example than that of Juan Perón; easily the spitting image of everything fundamentally wrong with politics in South America at their most acrid and that was saying a lot. When Távora had read that Cipriano Reyes, the new face of Argentina's resurgent Peronism, he all but ripped the newspaper in half.; Barely a few decades removed and Brazil had to put up with these chauvinistic baboons all over again?

And what did it all mean? A generation of Argentine political acumen spent to sprint away from what Perón represented, just to hand it back to his heirs like he never even left? Populism gone rabid, nationalism gone cannibal and a foreign policy (a generous description at that) which was like to put the Southern Cone on the brink of war.; God damn them! Távora thought with intense frustration.
strings.BRA_latam_reactions.35.a: A familiar belligerent returns to South America.
strings.BRA_pres_70_debug.1.desc:
The Presidential candidates have been picked and announced. A fierce race now begins in Brazil for who will come out on top as campaigns kick into full gear. Campaigners go door to door convincing voters one by one on who to vote for. Great speeches are held in front of thousands to convince the popular masses, while backroom deals are held to give each candidate an edge. Meanwhile the military watches the campaign go on, their thoughts unknown to the public.

It is time to choose who you will campaing for.

strings.BRA_pres_70_debug.1.c: The only sensible solution, campaign for Braga!

strings.BRA_military_info_normal_tt:
Brazil's Armed Forces have been a constant source of concern for Brazil's government, even more so after the failed 1955 coup attempt. The military is plagued by debilitating Nepotism which impairs combat readiness, and Loyalty of military leadership is tenuous at best.

Internally, the military faces a power struggle between three groups: the pro-democracy £BRA_constitutionalists_texticon Constitutionalists, the moderate £BRA_sorbonne_texticon Sorbonne, and the antagonistic £BRA_hardliners_texticon Hardliners. The faction in control and level of military Loyalty will determine how much instability the military will tolerate before intervention is seen as the only option.

The President must act wisely, for their actions towards the military and on issues of national security will affect all of these properties.
strings.BRA_Adhemarist_military_info_tt:
Brazil's Armed Forces have been a constant source of concern for Brazil's government, even more so after the failed 1955 coup attempt. The military is plagued by debilitating Nepotism which impairs combat readiness, and Loyalty of military leadership is tenuous at best.

Internally, the military faces a power struggle between four groups: the pro-democracy £BRA_constitutionalists_texticon Constitutionalists, the moderate £BRA_sorbonne_texticon Sorbonne, the antagonistic £BRA_hardliners_texticon Hardliners, and the growing influence of the overtly political £BRA_psp_texticon Progressistas. The faction in control and level of military Loyalty will determine how much instability the military will tolerate before intervention is seen as the only option.

The President must act wisely, for their actions towards the military and on issues of national security will affect all of these properties.
strings.BRA_military_loyalty_tt_delay: Ever since the military coup which bore Brazil's Fourth Republic, the nation's armed forces have played an outsized role in its politics. The Lott administration has managed to appease the military's top brass, but if the political situation grows dire a disloyal military may choose to intervene.
strings.BRA_military_nepotism_tt_delay: Nepotism is a thorn in the side of Brazil's armed forces, the military is rife with inefficiencies and our soldiers lack proper oversight. Tackling this corruption will be a difficult task, but a necessary one if we are to be prepared for the next conflict.

strings.BRA_military_dominant_tt_delay: The dominant military faction controls how likely the military is to intervene due to political instability.
strings.BRA_military_hardliners_tt:
£BRA_hardliners_texticon Hardliners
--------------






{gethardlinerleader}
--------------
Known as “Goosesteppers” to their detractors, the Hardliners are the most antagonistic faction to Brazilian democracy. The group has existed for decades, held together by their common ambition. Many of those that forced Vargas from power were Hardliners, the same officers and generals who aimed to take power in the failed 1955 coup. As long as the Hardliners are promised wealth and power, they will remain loyal, but they won't ever be sated for long.
strings.BRA_military_sorbonne_tt:
£BRA_sorbonne_texticon Sorbonne
--------------






{getsorbonneleader}
--------------
The Sorbonne are the so-called moderates of the Brazilian military, favoring the status quo. The primary concern of the Sorbonne is ensuring a stable Brazil that ensures their checks come in on time and they can retire with a sizable pension. While they may lack the ambition of the Hardliners and the ideological devotion of the Constitutionalists, what the Sorbonne do have is pragmatism.
strings.BRA_military_constitutionalists_tt:
£BRA_constitutionalists_texticon Constitutionalists
--------------






{getconstitutionalistleader}
--------------
Founded by Marshal Lott during the attempted coup of 1955, the Constitutionalists support the continuation of the Fourth Republic and democracy, no matter its leader. The Constitutionalists aim to quell any suggestion of a military solution to Brazil's woes, and will shield the President to intervention to the best of their abilities.
strings.BRA_military_progressistas_tt:
£BRA_psp_texticon Progressistas
--------------






{getprogleader}
--------------
In truth, the only thing that unites the so-called Progressistas is money. Bound together by a chain of favors, gifts, and promises forged by President Adhemar de Barros, the Progressistas are loyal to country first and the PSP a close second. Loyalty is a fickle thing, however - if the patronage which the Progressistas depend on was to end, the faction might disappear with it.

strings.BRA_military_frota_coup: The military have decided to take matters into their own hands...
strings.BRA_military_reassure_brass_desc: We will take the time to sit down with military leaders, reiterating our commitment to solving Brazil's problems.
strings.BRA_military_promote_loyal_desc: Though back channels, we will ensure that officers of the Constitutionalist faction are rewarded for their loyalty. In turn, they will quiet any talks of military subversion.
strings.BRA_military_oversight_desc: We will order a regular administrative inspection to ensure our military is in fighting shape. This will give us a chance to target ineffective or unqualified leaders.
strings.BRA_military_audit_desc: A complete audit of the military's books will let us uncover deep-rooted cronyism, but such close oversight will undoubtably be unpopular among those who are already wary of our administration.
strings.BRA_military_adhemar_pay_off_loyal_desc: Adhemar will arrange some off-the-books payments to officers amicable to the PSP. In turn, they will quiet any talks of military subversion.
strings.BRA_military_adhemar_smuggle_out_some_st: Adhemar will sell off some surplus military supplies to foreign bidders with the understanding that some of that money will kick back to him directly.
strings.BRA_hold_competency_test_desc: As the South American Cold War rages on, we can not afford to have incompetent officers dragging us down - and too many have had it far too easy for too long. While it will be unpopular with them, it will produce a stronger officer core.
strings.BRA_military_impending_coup_desc: We have received word that the military is plotting to coup our government unless we are able to get a better hold on the political situation. It is imperitive that we secure their loyalty or improve conditions before it is too late.
strings.BRA_military_impending_coup_2_desc: Despite Lott's promises, conditions have worsened. The plans for a coup are being put back into motion, and there is little we can do but wait for the worst to occur.
strings.BRA_military_impending_coup_trigger: Brazil's Stability or military Loyalty has improved
strings.BRA_military_impending_coup_fail_effect: The military will stage a coup!
strings.BRA_military_nation_chaos_action: Decisions to increase Hardliner influence will be enabled
strings.BRA_military_nation_chaos_action_2: Decisions to increase £BRA_sorbonne_texticon Sorbonne influence will be enabled
strings.BRA_military_dictatorship: Brazil is under a military dictatorship.
strings.BRA_sorbonne_ally_politicians_desc: The Senado was shut down as an act of necessity, and some of its members recognize this. Some have openly supported our mission to restore peace to Brazil, and surely others can be convinced that we made the right decision.
strings.BRA_sorbonne_replace_garrisons_desc: Many of the so-called Hardliners act out of personal ambition rather than ideological conviction. Reshuffling key garrisons will ensure that any selfish plots are rightly thwarted.
strings.BRA_sorbonne_undermine_hardliners_desc: The Hardliners have served their purpose in saving Brazil from anarchy, but now they wish to drag it into tyranny. The rational among us know the truth: These power-hungry officers are not Brazil's friends, nor are they acting in her best interest.
strings.BRA_hardliners_purge_sorbonne_desc: The moderate Sorbonne have thus far been tolerated due to their similar goals, but that is no longer the case. Foolishly, they wish to schedule elections, but to what end? Brazil will soon find herself facing the same problems as before, and next time we may not be so lucky. We must purge our ranks from these weaklings.
strings.BRA_hardliners_promote_hardliners_desc: Promoting likeminded officers into key positions within the armed forces will allow us to consolidate our grasp and expand our influence further.
strings.BRA_hardliners_crackdown_politics_desc: Breaking up on unsanctioned political meetings, filled with the sort of rabble-rousers who set Brazil on her perilous course, will give us breathing room and help keep our enemies unorganized.
strings.BRA_increase_loyalty_timer_desc: The so-called coup was the result of Brazil's politicians flagrantly ignoring the military's warnings. Now that we have righted Brazil's course, this trust has started to rebuild.
strings.BRA_arrest_dissidents_timer_desc: The mission of the military is to restore order to Brazil... and purging the dissident cancer is part and parcel of that job.
strings.BRA_kubitschek_goals_plan_info:
The 2º Programa de Metas represents Kubitschek's ambitious development goals for Brazil, carrying on where his first term left off.

Hand-picked from the upper echelons of government and the private sector by Kubitschek at the beginning of each year, the advisors of the Conselho do Desenvolvimento shape the administration's approach to the £BRA_JK_development_texticon Development, £BRA_JK_infrastructure_texticon Infrastructure, £BRA_JK_energy_texticon Energy, £BRA_JK_education_texticon Education, and £BRA_JK_healthcare_texticon Healthcare targets which are also drafted in January.

Ebullient and determined, Kubitchek relies on the Optimism of the £BRA_JK_people_texticon People, £BRA_JK_business_texticon Business, and £BRA_JK_creditors_texticon Foreign Creditors to achieve his vision. Setting ambitious yearly targets will encourage this Optimism, even moreso when they are met. If Kubitschek's government fails to deliver, however, the Optimism and national unity he relies on will fade.

strings.BRA_gp_speech_pn: Brazil is a future-minded nation, this was made clear with the completion of the Rio-São Paulo Line, the first railway of its kind in the Americas.

strings.BRA_gp_cd_0_trait:
Public Health Crusader
  - Healthcare Goal Progress Bonus: +15%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_0_desc: A PSP man, Pinotti is a trained medic and sanitarist. As director of the Brazilian National Malaria Service, he pioneered chloroquinized salt during the 1950s to help eradicate malaria. Although he's not a PSD or PTB man, he's worked with Kubitschek before on medical matters and is a close ally in this regard. If Kubitschek wants to improve Brazil's healthcare, Pinotti is a needed ally, and he can even improve ties with Adhemar and the PSP as a bonus.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_1_trait:
Airline Executive
  - Unlocks Ready Airways for the Future focus branch.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_1_desc: Erik is a businessman working for Varig Airlines, the first domestic airline in Brazil that was founded in 1927. It is Brazil's leading airline and its only international one. Erik has done a lot to expand Varig operations and expand Varig's fleet of aircraft. He will be an important ally if Kubitschek wants to focus on improving air travel, especially in the matter of new airports.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_2_trait:
Picasso of Concrete
  - Mega Project Construction Speed: +5%
  - Mega Project Optimism Bonus: +15%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_2_desc: Oscar Niemeyer is considered to be one of the key figures in the development of modern architecture. His greatest projects include many public buildings in Brasília, like the National Congress, the Presidential Palace, and the world-famous Cathedral of Brasília. Niemeyer's ties with communist groups may make some look at him with suspicious eyes, but his friendship with Kubitschek and intimate knowledge of architecture will surely bring weight to any project he is attached to.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_3_trait:
Structuralist Planner
  - Mega Project Construction Speed: +10%
SUDENE Czar
  Northeast
    - Monthly Industry Growth: +0.10%
    - Monthly Mech. Rate Growth: +0.10%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_3_desc: A PTB man, Furtado worked for Kubitschek in the previous development council and was a key ally of Lott for his economic plans. He's a supporter of Keynesianism and structuralist economics. In particular, he continues to emphasize his dream of pulling up Brazil's northeast so it can be put on the same economic playing field as the rest of Brazil. He is also one of the most distinguished intellectuals in the country, and was previously Director of the Brazilian Development Bank.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_4_desc: One of the most important leaders of the PSD, Tancredo was an economics advisor in Kubitschek's last term and also led the Ministry of Economics during Lott's government. His skills and knowledge in economics will surely be an asset to the Development Council and his appointment will help the Council navigate through many political entanglements, as his leadership was held in high esteem during his times as congressman, advisor, and minister.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_5_trait:
Constitutionalist Background
  - Weekly £BRA_constitutionalists_texticon Constitutionalist support: +0.25
The Oil is Ours
  - Energy Goal Progress Bonus: +10%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_5_desc: General Alves is a constitutionalist officer and the leader of the First Army, headquartered in Rio by Kubitschek at Goulart and Edna Lott's advice. He's been appointed to ensure that the reformed military continues to support the President, and thus has earned a say on what Kubitschek does. He is also not a member of any political party, making him effectively non-aligned, and thus a safe, apolitical choice that can be trusted to be unfailingly loyal.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_6_trait:
Army Liaison
  - Military Loyalty grows over time
strings.BRA_gp_cd_6_desc: One of Brazil's most decorated marshals, Cardoso began his career mere weeks before WW1 ended, then saw action in the 1924 Paulista Revolt. He fought in the Brazilian Revolution of 1930, commanded an artillery battalion of the Brazilian Expeditionary Force in WW2, and then commanded a division in São Paulo. Waldemar has seen everything the Brazilian Army has had to deal with for the past fifty years, and while no longer active as a field marshal, he is well-respected with plenty of business connections, making him a good ally for gaining military support.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_7_trait:
Auto Baron
  Southeast
    - Monthly Industry Growth: +0.20%
  South
    - Monthly Industry Growth: +0.20%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_7_desc: Schulz-Wenk is the owner of Volkswagen do Brazil, one of the largest car manufacturers in the nation. Brazilian-German tensions are high and most trade between them is non-existent, but Volkswagen vehicles are one of the few exceptions. Kubitschek intends to increase Volkswagen operations in Brazil, and Schulz-Wenk will be a key ally in ensuring the further growth of the car industry and helping strengthen Brazil's improving economy.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_8_trait:
Media Magnate
  - Goal Failture Optimism Penalty: -30%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_8_desc: Mário Wallace Simonsen has been described as one of the most influential businessmen in the country, as he's the main owner of the television network TV Excelsior. Other business includes investment in many of Brazil's young airway companies. Mário's unwavering support for the growth of national industry and technologies landed him in a leading position in Kubitschek's Development Council. The President needs all media support he can get, and Simonsen's connections and fame will surely help.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_9_trait:
Trailblazing Pedagogue
  - Education Goal Progress Bonus: +15%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_9_desc: An educator and philosopher, Paulo Freire has ties to the Christian socialist faction in the PTB but is criticized by many for his Marxist beliefs and writings. His goals are to improve literacy rates across the country and ensure the large-scale application of his theories and models of education. Freire and Kubitschek agree that education policies were mostly ignored during JK's previous term, and now is time to correct this mistake, justifying Freire's position in the Development Council.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_10_trait:
Developmental Economist
  - Development Goal Progress Bonus: +15%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_10_desc: A PSD man, Campos is a major economist in Brazil and an admirer of Hayek's works. Despite this, he has consistently supported Varguist economic nationalism. He supported the creation of the National Bank for Economic Development (BNDES), and many emerging industries in the country. Now as Kubitschek's economic advisor, he will continue similar policies, most notably trying to merge Kubitschek's developmentalist policies with local businesses.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_11_desc: Dante Pellacani the current President of the General Command of Workers, and an officeholder in the National Confederation of Workers in Industry is a key figure in Brazil's union's. Both groups are an immense political force within the PCB and PTB. Pellacani cut his ties to the PCB after the party briefly supported Adhemar de Barros and found a new home within the PTB. Since then he has moved uo the ladder, becoming a key player in the PTB and with a multitude of contacts within the general Brazilian labor movement and is still incredibly popular among both union leadership and politicians. However there are many in the PSD that are  wary of having such a controversial figure in the council, due to history of participating in strikes and having been arrested multiple times. However both Goulart and Lott have voiced support for the man and there may be very little chance of keeping some of the PTB in the coalition without the appointment of Pellacani.
strings.BRA_gp_cd_12_trait:
Agrarian Reformer
  - Monthly Mech. Rate Growth: +0.10%
strings.BRA_gp_cd_12_desc: The leading figure in the left-wing of the PDC, Plínio is considered to be one of the foremost proponents of agricultural and land reform. His career was forged in São Paulo's politics, and he soon was elected as a federal congressman. In Congress, he was part of the Committees on Economics, Agricultural Policy, and Social Legislation, working closely with the PSD and Lott's government. In light of Plínio's talents in negotiation, oratory, and legal knowledge, Kubitschek is ready to use those same talents in the Development Council.
strings.BRA_gp_weeks: at the end of the year, in [?temp_weeks|0] weeks.
