strings.BRA_VEN.2.desc:
The throbbing pain on his knees was familiar to Carlos. He remembered it from that morning with Pa, hiking up Pico Alto in Ceará. The view was familiar, too, with rolling blankets of fog surrounding the hillsides, and orange sun hatched onto the trees.

A nice view to build a base around, he supposed, marching towards the red flag hanging off a branch ahead. From green shadows appeared the iron glint of gun barrels. It was well known to the SNI that the Colombian Revolutionary Union had forces embedded in the mountains of Mérida, across the border in Venezuelan territory. To “facilitate cooperation,” it was said. The rifles pointed to his every side didn't inspire that sentiment.

“Of course we have heard of the fascists at the border,” spat one fighter, flies dotting his face. “We were the ones to verify your intelligence.”

“And what will you do?” Carlos paced, guns trailing his steps.

“Is it your business?” Asked the oldest of the guerrilleros, gaunt and covered in gauze.

“We have utmost concern for the security of Venezuelan democracy,” Carlos declared, earning snickers from all around. Good. Laughs were oil for diplomacy.

“Not more than us. Venezuela is our closest friend,” said the senior. “We will help them against the invasion, as much for their sake as for ours.”

Carlos clasped his hands, and dug out a map. “Then you won't have a problem making a short trek to El Vijía, as well.”

The guerrilleros glanced at where he pointed. “The air base in Zulia?”

“Involved in the coup, we believe. Pay them a visit, won't you?”

They shook their hands on it, and Carlos descended back down the trails of gray clouds. The ghost of their guns pinned to his back never left.
strings.BRA_VEN.2.a: The guerrilla poises for a fight.
strings.BRA_VEN.3.desc:
The air stank with sweat and iron, and Carlos was having a bad day. He dangled his gun between his legs.

“I know you really, really want it to stop. Can see it in your eyes.”

A brief silence, filled by the mewls of that man, the man they'd captured, SIM Dominican bastard, that they'd tied to a chair here on a pretty, newly-painted shack outside of San Cristóbal, where the screams wouldn't be heard.

Pop! Rodrigo pulled nails clean like a mother removing bandaids. He shushed the Dominican, put his bloody hand on the vomit-stained gag. It failed to quell the squealing, and so Carlos waved and Rodrigo removed the gag, and the prisoner convulsed between strained, deep breaths and groans. His third removed nail landed with a neat clank on Rodrigo's tin plate.

“Are we going to lose you too?” Carlos asked, nodding to the other prisoners. One was sprawled on the floor, simmering in his own blood. Made a stupid move and forced Carlos to shoot him. The other didn't have the stomach and passed out on the first nail. They didn't have enough cold water to wake him.

“I'm not,” the man mumbled. “I'm not Dominican.”

“And we're Brazilians in Venezuela. Don't care who you are. We care for information. For the last time: What do you know about the attack on San Cristóbal?”

“They have eyes on me.”

“We can protect you from harm,” Carlos lied.

“I can't,” he screamed. “They know where my mother lives. They know where I live.”

“We know that too.” Carlos lifted his gun, and finished the interrogation with a shot to the neck and chest. Another bullet was spent on the unconscious victim.
strings.BRA_VEN.3.a: Another dud. Let's hatch a better plan after disposing of these.
strings.BRA_VEN.4.desc:
ULTRA SECRETO
SOMENTE PARA OS OLHOS DO PRESIDENTE

DO ESCRITÓRIO DO SERVIÇO NACIONAL DE INFORMAÇÕES
Subject: Imminent coup in Venezuela

1. Rising levels of military activity along the Colombian border suggest that the coup attempt is expected to occur in a matter of days. While it is not currently within our means to pinpoint a specific timeframe and location for the initial assault, suspicious troop movements all across the country ensure that no area can remain outside our vigilance.

2. With potential insurgent forces lying in the vicinity of every major population center, it is of paramount importance that these isolated groups must not be allowed to communicate with each other. Striking at the rebels' organisational structure is to be considered our number one priority if we are to prevent their success.

3. Despite the best efforts of our local field agents, constant sabotage operations from meddling fascist parties have left the issue of the impending conflict uncertain. Given its proximate nature, it is almost certain that whatever operations we have already conducted will unfortunately have to suffice.

4. Nonetheless, we remain confident that our mission in Venezuela was, by and large, a success, and will prove critical to the region's defense, should worse come to worst.

For the time being, the cards are in the hands of the local government.
strings.BRA_VEN.5.desc:
Carlos granted a passing smile at the pair of armed guerrillas he met along the way, earning not much more than a vaguely annoyed grunt by way of response as they kept driving a restrained, hooded figure in military fatigues. He'd gotten used to this treatment: most of the people here held nothing but either contempt or confusion over his presence among them; and that was for those even aware of it. Not that he minded, though. He was in quite a good mood now that he had just finished filing his report, and had decided to take a final stroll outside before his upcoming departure from Venezuelan soil.

By now, most of the bodies had already been cleared from the Air Base's floor, with the remaining stragglers still clumsily ordered in lines of nameless bags in front of a nearby hangar. The other lucky few had either been picked off as they tried to flee, had scattered to the hills, or probably fallen to an ambush along the banks of the Turbio. Either way, the putschists had failed to grasp a proper hold on the city. Whatever lingering pockets of resistance would either be dead or arrested by the next few hours.

His intel had been correct. Hours ago, Castro León's goons had tried to seize Barquisimeto from the southwest, with the attempt finding an unfortunate stop at the hands of the pro-government militias that had received advance warning. Without this crucial logistical line to Puerto Cabello, it was only a matter of time before insurgent forces east of Valencia would fall like dominoes. He had already heard reports of disorganized rebel cells in San Felipe getting caught off-guard by DIGEPOL raids.

Fighting was still raging in most of the country, yet for all intents and purposes, the coup had been smothered in the cradle before it could even reach Caracas. Though it was a close call, he couldn't help but feel a sense of satisfaction at this turn of events. His own part in it, though, was over. He smiled, making his way back inside to pack his things.
strings.BRA_VEN.5.a: In most minds, his part will never have even existed in the first place.
strings.BRA_VEN.6.desc:
ULTRA SECRETO
SOMENTE PARA OS OLHOS DO PRESIDENTE

DO ESCRITÓRIO DO SERVIÇO NACIONAL DE INFORMAÇÕES
Subject: Report on the coup attempt in Venezuela

1. Despite finding initial success in seizing the city of San Cristóbal, insurgent forces led by former General Jesús María Castro León failed to build sufficient momentum to push toward other key areas, even after being shortly joined by Colombian reactionary dissidents from Cúcuta and the support of Iberian intelligence.

2. Facing disorderly communication and unreliable supply lines, attempts to capture cities such as Maracaibo, Barquisimeto, and Maracay were all met with failure, thwarting any hope for the putschists to gain enough hold to undertake a decisive assault on the country's capital of Caracas.

3. Efforts from the coup leadership to regroup and organize their scattered forces were further paralysed by a crippling worker strike in their home base of San Cristóbal. After hours of continued fighting with government loyalists, Castro León ordered his troops to stand down, and is now in the process of being incarcerated in the Cuartel San Carlos while he awaits a military trial for high treason.

4. With the position of Venezuela's democratic government secured in major part thanks to our activities in the region, this fortuitous outcome is not only expected to bolster our diplomatic ties with local authorities, but also represent an increase in trust from our American partners; all while proving to be a serious blow to Iberian efforts to pull the nation into their own sphere.
strings.BRA_VEN.7.desc:
As soon as he'd finished typing the last words on the fax machine, Carlos slumped back on his chair. He briefly considered catching a few minutes of sleep, ignoring the better part of his mind warning him otherwise. He wondered how much time he truly had. For now, in the dead of the night, the streets of Tamaca were still eerily quiet; though by morning, the chaos down south would have probably spilled over here too. At least, he thought, he still had the luxury of rewarding himself with a smoke.

Earlier in the day, the putschists had seized control of the air base back in Barquisimeto, while he had barely managed to scrape away with his life. By now, the entire city was probably under their control. He pondered his own options. With the whole west of the country falling into rebel hands, any hope of fleeing toward Colombia was compromised. His only hope would be to continue northward and chance upon a ferry that would bring him to Curaçao.

For now, he enjoyed a quiet moment of pause, the fumes delightfully filling his lungs as he strolled to fetch a jerrycan laying in the other corner of the safehouse. Neatly gathered at the center of the basement was a significant stack of records. Mission briefings. Networks of contacts. Intel files of potentially useful informants. Guerrilla boys he had sent to their deaths. Forged passports. Associates from other cells. He shook his head, before starting to pour the gasoline.

His eyes lingered on some of the faces that were slowly getting tainted by the thick liquid. Even now, a part of him still hoped that the radio would spark with anything but the same static it had sprouted for the past few hours. He had tried in vain to reach his fellows in San Cristóbal, Maracaibo, or even Cabudares. Nothing to comfort him that they'd had much better luck than he. He sighed, drawing one last puff from the cigarette before it met the document pile, watching as the flames swiftly engulfed his efforts for the past few months.
strings.BRA_VEN.7.a: He still had a long night ahead of him.
strings.BRA_VEN.8.desc:
ULTRA SECRETO
SOMENTE PARA OS OLHOS DO PRESIDENTE

DO ESCRITÓRIO DO SERVIÇO NACIONAL DE INFORMAÇÕES
Subject: Report on the coup attempt in Venezuela

1. Hours after seizing the city of San Cristóbal, insurgent forces led by former General Jesús María Castro León managed to secure control of most of the western half of the country. With backing from allies in the neighbouring Colombian city of Cúcuta, the putschists proceeded to capture other key areas, such as the southern Vega de Aza road or a major airbase in El Vigía.

2. A worker strike in San Cristóbal, hoping to cripple logistical efforts, was promptly crushed by local rebel troops. With loyalist military personnel unable to easily threaten the coup's home base, Castro's León mutineers found little to no resistance as they went on to subdue critical cities such as Maracaibo and Barquisimeto, further pushing toward the heart of the country.

3. Mere 12 hours after the fighting began, Caracas officially fell, with the government being promptly evacuated when rebel forces entered the confines of the city. With the capital firmly under their control, the coup leadership wasted no time in relocating their headquarters to the vacated Palacio de Miraflores, where Castro León has now been sworn President.

4. Owing to the total collapse of the Venezuelan democratic apparatus, this outcome is a disaster for our diplomatic efforts in the region, with the putsch leadership openly hostile to our administration. While the country is now set to grow further ties to the Iberian sphere, we must also expect American authorities to be seriously displeased by our mishandling of the situation.
strings.BRA_VEN.9.desc:
The man in the brown zoot suit entered the embassy building at 10:23 PM, Sunday, and had yet to be seen again five days later. At 11:59 AM on Friday, his status as an asset for DIGEPOL was terminated, his name crossed over, and his handler reprimanded. Promptly, a cable was sent from the Venezuelans to Brazilian authorities; the Iberian embassy was harboring a defector.

“Nothing we can do about it,” it was said. “The pig's got diplomatic refuge.”

A cigarette was smothered. “And we won't be stepping on the Iberians' toes over this shit. Their defector, their problem.”

It seemed a closed matter for Brasília's intelligence bigwigs, and the Venezuelans wouldn't make a big deal of it, if just to save face. It didn't reach the ears of any higher offices, let alone the president, and nobody wanted the international incident that would erupt. The meeting was closed until a young officer spoke up.

“Could we not take advantage of this? We could make it up to the Venezuelans by monitoring the embassy, letting them know of any other suspicious visitors.”

A senior took a pause. “What do we gain?”

He grinned. “They'll owe us a favor.”
strings.BRA_VEN.9.a: And in the world of intelligence, favors are everything.
strings.BRA_VEN.9.b: Shut the upstart down. This is the Venezuelan's mess, not ours.
